There would then be no concern that she would waive in favor of her husband, because the husband's debt to her would stand directly encumbered to the noteholder under Rabbi Natan's rule. This argument avoids the Shach's objection and all the difficulties discussed above. One might respond, with difficulty, that selling a one hundred dinar ketubah for ten does not involve ribbit, because the purchaser is buying an uncertain asset. But if the injured party is presently owed only ten and the woman executes a note for a larger amount because collection is uncertain, perhaps that increase would be treated as ribbit. Even this is strained. The Hagahot Ashri in Ketubot, chapter Af Al Pi, explains that when a husband adds one fifth to a ketubah there is no ribbit because the increase is not tied to time. If the obligation becomes payable immediately, he must pay the entire amount immediately. Here too the additional face amount is not compensation for time. If she were widowed immediately, the full amount would become collectible at once. The discount reflects only the uncertainty of whether the condition for collection will ever occur. Furthermore, in the case where she injured her husband, the Gemara says that when the ketubah exceeds the damages she cannot sell it to him because Rabbi Meir forbids leaving a wife without a ketubah. Suppose the damages are fifty and the ketubah is one hundred. Beit din could award the husband fifty dinars of the ketubah at a present speculative value of, say, twenty five. The remaining twenty five of his damages could be represented by a separate promissory note secured against the remaining fifty of the ketubah. The husband could then sell that note for its speculative value, perhaps twelve dinars. This would not make divorce easier in his eyes, because if he divorces her he must still pay the full remaining fifty, twenty five to her and twenty five to the noteholder. Yet the husband would gain the additional twelve dinars from selling the note, over and above the fifty of the ketubah that was judicially awarded to him at its present speculative value. The note purchaser would have no fear of waiver because Rabbi Natan's rule would directly secure his debt against the remaining ketubah. This is a clear proof for the Ramban and Ran. Examine it carefully. See also what I wrote above in siman 66 concerning the Mishnah's statement that if she is divorced she becomes liable. What novelty does that teach? And how can the Mishnah state categorically that she is liable? She could presumably waive her ketubah to the husband to defeat the injured party. The Mishnah's certainty therefore indicates that she cannot waive the portion encumbered to the injured party under Rabbi Natan's rule. That is precisely its teaching: after divorce she is definitely liable, without any possibility of eliminating the claim through waiver. We now return to Tosafot and the Rosh and ask which view they follow. It appears that the logic of Torah law supports the Ramban and Ran, quite apart from the proof I wrote at the beginning of this siman from the Rosh and Tur. I explained there at length that they too hold that the intermediate creditor cannot waive the debt, although I suggested that their basis is not specifically Rabbi Natan's rule but another principle. Tosafot asks how the woman can waive her ketubah, since it is forbidden to keep a wife without a ketubah. Tosafot answers that the husband can write her a new ketubah after the waiver. Tosafot then asks that the woman would still owe the purchaser damages under the law of dina d'garmi for causing the purchased ketubah to be lost, and answers that since she presently has no property from which to pay, this does not help the purchaser and the entire arrangement remains futile. This is very difficult. The initial acquisition was a purchase of her right to eventual ketubah payment. Even if she waives the first ketubah, the husband must write her a new one. She could then sell the new ketubah for its present speculative value to satisfy the damages she caused by waiving the first. If she waived again, he would again have to write a ketubah. The cycle would continue until actual collection became possible. Thus the purchaser does not necessarily lose anything merely because she waives the first ketubah. The Maharsha appears to have intended this difficulty, although his words are somewhat compressed. It is difficult to answer that before waiving she could collusively execute a promissory note to a third party, so that when the husband writes the new ketubah that third party's earlier note would take priority over the purchaser's damages claim. If we were concerned about such a device, the Gemara could never prove Shmuel's rule that a seller can waive a sold note. One cannot force the woman to sell her ketubah in a single instant. A day before the sale she could execute a note to someone else, and if it contained a broad acquisition clause, all her later property might already be encumbered. Yet the commentators repeatedly explain that we do not ordinarily suspect a person of arranging such a fraudulent collusion merely to injure another. With the husband himself there is also no concern that she will simply execute a debt equal to the ketubah in his favor, because that would make divorce easy in his eyes and would violate the prohibition against living with a wife who lacks a meaningful ketubah. Tosafot itself, s.v. "such as," indicates that only the special circumstance caused by her own act of injury permits the exceptional arrangement. Therefore this kind of artificial note cannot explain Tosafot. Nor is it persuasive to say that after the waiver the husband could evade the new ketubah by transferring away all his assets before writing it. If that were the concern, Tosafot need not say that she waives the ketubah entirely. She could simply release the purchaser's rights while retaining her ketubah against the husband, and he could continue living with her. Moreover, we do not generally assume such a deliberate scheme to strip the husband of assets merely to defeat the purchaser.

To resolve Tosafot, there are two possible approaches. First, it may be said that when the Gemara states that with respect to her husband she will certainly waive, it does not mean only a waiver directly to the husband. The same concern exists after his death with respect to his heirs, because she is close to them and prefers that the money remain with them rather than pass to a stranger. This must in fact be said according to the Rambam, who holds that while a woman remains married she has no legal power to waive the ketubah to her husband. How then can the Gemara say that with respect to her husband she will certainly waive? See the Beit Shmuel. It is strained to say that the Rambam adopts Tosafot's device that the husband first divorces her, she then waives, and he later remarries her, for the Rambam rules without qualification that a married woman who injures another is difficult to collect from, while the wife of a kohen is not difficult to collect from because she can sell her ketubah, even though a kohen cannot divorce and then remarry her. I discussed the Tosafot issue in my novellae and above in siman 67. Rather, the Gemara must mean that after the husband's death she will waive the ketubah to his heirs because she is close to them and prefers them to an outsider. Tosafot can likewise accept this understanding. The Ramban's question then immediately arises: why should she be able to waive to the heirs when the ketubah is directly encumbered to the injured party under Rabbi Natan's rule? One must answer in accordance with the Ran that while the husband is alive the time for collection has not arrived and the ketubah is only a contingent future claim. Yet if the concern is specifically waiver to the heirs after the husband's death, the debt is then fixed and complete, and at that point the heirs should be directly obligated to the injured party under Rabbi Natan's rule. Tosafot therefore answers differently: she will waive to her husband during his lifetime, and he will write her a new ketubah. We may now say that Tosafot holds, as the Maharshal explains, that according to the view that liability for dina d'garmi is a rabbinic penalty, Rabbi Natan's rule does not apply to that liability. I wrote above that the same type of distinction appears with a moser according to those who understand dina d'garmi as a penalty. Tosafot holds in several places that dina d'garmi is a penalty. Thus Tosafot's answer works as follows. When she waives the first ketubah she becomes liable to the purchaser for the loss under dina d'garmi. If the purchaser then seeks to reach the new ketubah that the husband writes for her, she can wait until the husband dies and waive that new ketubah to the heirs. At that point the heirs are not directly obligated to the purchaser under Rabbi Natan's rule, because the purchaser's claim against her is only the penal liability of dina d'garmi, to which Rabbi Natan does not apply. The purchaser therefore loses. Those who adopt this distinction can derive support from our sugya, since they accept Tosafot's question and answer and need a way to avoid the problem just described. Yet the reason cannot simply be that a rabbinic debt never falls under Rabbi Natan's rule. The Shach correctly argues that when the Sages created monetary obligations they generally fashioned them after Torah law. Indeed, instead of asking where in the Talmud we find Rabbi Natan in a rabbinic obligation, one can point to the opposite. In the case of one who was owed money by his brother, the Gemara says that we do not combine two stringencies in a ketubah. Rashi explains that one of the relevant leniencies is due to the ketubah being rabbinic, which shows that Rabbi Natan's rule by itself can operate even with a rabbinic ketubah. Even according to the Rif and those who explain that passage as referring to two enactments rather than two stringencies, the enactment of the Geonim concerning collection of movables can coexist with Rabbi Natan's rule. And we rule that a ketubah is rabbinic while Rabbi Natan still applies to it in appropriate circumstances. Rather, the distinction concerning dina d'garmi is that Rabbi Natan operates where the debtor's property is firmly and absolutely encumbered. According to the view that dina d'garmi is a penalty, if the tortfeasor dies before standing in judgment, the penalty is not imposed on his heirs even if he left encumbered property. There is therefore no fixed property lien at the moment of the damaging act from which Rabbi Natan can derive a direct obligation. The point is not simply that the obligation is rabbinic, but that a penalty of this type does not yet create an absolute lien. Even if this approach can explain some authorities, it is difficult to attribute it to Tosafot, for we do not find Tosafot explicitly stating anywhere that Rabbi Natan does not apply to dina d'garmi, and such a significant rule should have been explained. More importantly, this cannot explain the Rosh. The Rosh states explicitly in Bava Kamma that dina d'garmi is ordinary monetary law and not a penalty, following the Ramban. That is why the Rosh must distinguish between grama and garmi, a distinction that would be unnecessary according to the view that the entire category is merely a penalty. See below in siman 386. There is therefore another possible route in Tosafot. Tosafot may agree with the view of the Tosafot Yeshanim in Ketubot 19b, s.v. "such as," cited in Hagahot HaRosh and by many authorities, and see Bach at the end of siman 85 and Shach at the beginning of this siman. According to that view, Rabbi Natan's rule applies only if Levi was already indebted to Shimon before Shimon borrowed from Reuven. If Shimon first borrowed from Reuven and only afterward lent to Levi, Levi does not become directly obligated to Reuven under Rabbi Natan's rule. Accordingly Tosafot is readily explained. As noted, Tosafot could not answer that the woman will simply waive the original ketubah to the husband's heirs, because once the husband dies the ketubah becomes a fixed debt and the heirs would then be directly obligated to the purchaser under Rabbi Natan. Tosafot therefore says that she waives the first ketubah while the husband is alive and the husband then writes her a new ketubah. Her liability to the purchaser under dina d'garmi arises at the moment she waives the first ketubah. The replacement ketubah is created only afterward. Thus the purchaser's claim against her precedes the husband's new ketubah obligation to her. Under the Tosafot Yeshanim's view, a debt of the ultimate debtor created after the first creditor's claim does not become subject to Rabbi Natan. Therefore when the husband later dies she can waive the replacement ketubah to his heirs without the purchaser being able to invoke Rabbi Natan. This resolves the entire chain. This also explains another difficulty. When a woman sells her ketubah she ordinarily does not lose the right of ketubat benin dichrin, whereas a complete waiver may destroy that right. Why then are we certain she will waive? According to what has just been explained, the concern can be that she will waive to the heirs after the relevant sequence has been arranged, and the effect on ketubat benin dichrin can be understood accordingly. The same approach explains Tosafot's question based on Rabbi Meir, who holds that at the end of cohabitation a woman cannot waive the minimum ketubah. At first glance, why is this difficult? Rabbi Meir prevents waiver of the basic two hundred, but if her ketubah were four hundred she could certainly waive two hundred while retaining the required minimum. Since Tosafot already says the husband can write her a new ketubah, let him write the replacement first, leaving her with four hundred, and she can then waive the two hundred that she sold to the purchaser. That would preserve the minimum ketubah. According to our explanation, however, that arrangement would not work. If the husband writes the replacement ketubah before the waiver, then when she later waives the sold ketubah and becomes liable to the purchaser under dina d'garmi, the husband's replacement ketubah obligation already exists. The purchaser's new damages claim would then be later than the replacement ketubah and Rabbi Natan's rule would attach to it. She could not defeat the purchaser by later waiving to the heirs. Tosafot therefore needs the replacement ketubah to be written only after the first waiver. The purchaser's damages claim then precedes the new ketubah obligation, so Rabbi Natan does not attach under the Tosafot Yeshanim's temporal rule. Tosafot adds that if Rabbi Meir prevents waiver at the end of cohabitation, the husband can divorce her and she can waive, and afterward he can remarry her. The intention need not be that she waits until after the divorce to waive, for then the ketubah debt is already fixed and Rabbi Natan's rule would apply. Rather, she waives in anticipation of immediate divorce. Rabbi Meir's objection is to a husband continuing to live with a wife after she has waived the minimum ketubah. If the waiver is immediately followed by divorce, and if he later remarries her with a valid new ketubah, there is no ongoing marriage without a ketubah. This is the proper understanding of Tosafot. See Beit Shmuel, Even HaEzer siman 65, seif katan 9. This also resolves a difficulty in the Maharsha. According to his understanding in Bava Batra 147, Rabbenu Tam holds that if a married woman sells her ketubah and later waives it in connection with divorce, she must pay the purchaser the full value. How then can Tosafot's answer work according to Rabbenu Tam? According to what I have written, she waives before the divorce, and the divorce follows immediately so that the husband does not continue living with her after the waiver. Thus the issue is not identical to a post divorce waiver of an already collectible ketubah. This framework also clarifies Tosafot in Ketubot 19, s.v. "where he injures others." I wrote above in siman 66, Tumim seif katan 351, that Tosafot in Bava Batra 147 can also be understood this way according to the Maharsha. Tosafot asks how, in the case of a found receipt, the woman can be believed because she has a migo that she could waive the ketubah. Perhaps she does not want to waive it to her husband and thereby suffer a real loss. The Maharsha wonders why she cannot simply trust her husband, just as in the receipt case she participates with him in collusion, as the Rosh explains. According to our analysis, the distinction is clear. Tosafot says in Bava Batra that a wife is embarrassed to sue her husband in beit din. Before she asks beit din to return the receipt to him, the husband can protect her by writing a replacement ketubah of the relevant amount. If the purchaser of the first ketubah later says, "You sold me a valid claim and now the receipt proves otherwise, return my money," and attempts to collect that refund from the replacement ketubah, she can wait until the husband's death and waive the replacement to the heirs. Rabbi Natan does not assist the purchaser, because if the sale is treated as void retroactively, his refund claim arose from the original sale, whereas the replacement ketubah was written only later at the time of the receipt's return. Under the temporal view of Tosafot Yeshanim, the later ketubah does not become directly encumbered to the earlier refund claim. But if she relies on the alternative of personally waiving the sold ketubah, the sequence is reversed. If she waives first, her husband may simply refuse afterward to write the replacement, and she is embarrassed to litigate against him, as Tosafot says. If he writes the replacement first and she then waives the sold ketubah, the purchaser's dina d'garmi claim arises only after the replacement ketubah. Rabbi Natan would then attach, and she could not defeat the purchaser by waiving to the heirs. Thus in either order she risks actual loss, and the migo of waiver is not equivalent to the receipt arrangement. This is precise. The same point resolves what I asked elsewhere according to Ri, who holds that even without dina d'garmi the seller must at least return the purchase money when she waives. Tosafot in Bava Batra says that if the baraita in Bava Metzia follows the view that does not adjudicate dina d'garmi, there is no difficulty for Ri. One might ask that even then the woman who waives must return the purchase money. The answer is that the entire problem involving waiver and the replacement ketubah arises where the damages obligation from the waiver comes only after the replacement ketubah, so Rabbi Natan can attach. If, however, the seller's obligation is merely to return the purchase money because the sale is treated as void retroactively on the implied condition that she not destroy the purchased right, then that refund debt is treated as arising from the original sale. It therefore precedes the replacement ketubah, and under the temporal rule Rabbi Natan does not attach. Furthermore, according to Tosafot's explanation that the power to waive resembles writing "I have received payment," partial receipt language has its own limitations. The difficulty therefore falls away.

And this appears from several points to be the direction of Tosafot: their view inclines toward Hagahot HaRosh and the authorities who hold that Rabbi Natan's rule does not attach where the ultimate debtor's obligation arose only after the middle creditor had already become indebted to the first creditor. These authorities have clear support from the analysis just given. Nevertheless, although this is a coherent and defensible reading of Tosafot, it is difficult to attribute the same temporal limitation to the Rosh. The Tur, his son, plainly does not accept it in many places, including this siman, siman 85, and siman 111. More decisively, in responsa, klal 35, concerning a man who gave sivlonot and the woman afterward married another, the Rosh rules that if dowry property was given to the second husband, the giver of the sivlonot can collect from that husband under Rabbi Natan's rule. Yet the sivlonot debt clearly preceded the second husband's later obligation arising from the dowry of the second marriage. This shows that the Rosh does not generally require the ultimate debtor's debt to predate the first creditor's claim. One might try to harmonize the sources by an approach similar to what must in any event be said concerning the Mordechai in Ketubot. The Mordechai says that if a woman waives her ketubah she does not lose ketubat benin dichrin. He asks how she can waive at all, since it is forbidden for a husband to live with his wife without a ketubah, and answers that she can waive conditionally: if the husband dies first, the ketubah is waived, but if he divorces her, he must still pay it. Since divorce does not become easier in his eyes, the concern underlying the ketubah enactment is preserved. Yet in Bava Kamma, in our sugya concerning a woman who injured her husband, the Mordechai asks why she cannot sell the ketubah to the husband on precisely such a condition, namely that if he dies she loses the ketubah but if he divorces her he must pay it. The fact that this proposal is rejected appears to show that according to Rabbi Meir even such a conditional reduction is prohibited because the Sages did not distinguish. The two passages in the Mordechai therefore seem contradictory. The proper explanation is that when the Mordechai invokes the principle that the Sages did not distinguish, he means that beit din should not advise or compel such a device. Since the Sages instituted the ketubah, beit din must reinforce that enactment rather than furnish techniques that weaken it. If judges themselves compel women to structure ketubot in a reduced or conditional form, others may learn from the practice and the rabbinic safeguard could be undermined. Beit din must therefore maintain the enactment with special firmness. But if husband and wife themselves, without any directive or coercion from beit din, arrange that the ketubah is waived only upon his death and remains fully payable upon divorce, beit din need not invalidate what they have done. The fundamental concern that divorce not become easy in his eyes is absent, since he must still pay the full ketubah if he divorces her. The Sages' rule against distinctions does not necessarily require beit din to interfere with every privately created arrangement that preserves the core purpose of the enactment. This reconciles the Mordechai. In Bava Kamma the entire discussion asks whether beit din should compel the woman to sell or restructure her ketubah in order to pay the injured party. In that context the Mordechai properly says that beit din may not weaken the ketubah enactment through such advice or coercion. In Ketubot, however, the woman herself waives conditionally without any judicial direction. There the Mordechai can recognize the arrangement because the husband remains fully liable upon divorce. If so, one could attempt a similar explanation of Tosafot and the Rosh. Beit din cannot initially instruct the woman to use this conditional device, because judges may not weaken the ketubah enactment. Yet when evaluating whether a purchaser will actually profit from buying her ketubah, we must fear that husband and wife themselves will privately arrange a new ketubah under which she is fully protected upon divorce but nothing is payable if he dies first. Such a private arrangement would not make divorce easier, and beit din need not stop it. The purchaser would then receive nothing, because no rational purchaser would pay even a perutah for a claim collectible only upon divorce from a husband with whom the wife continues living securely. Death is common, but divorce in such circumstances is not sufficiently probable to create meaningful market value. Although this explanation is intrinsically reasonable, it is difficult to fit into the language of Tosafot and the Rosh. If this were their intention, they did not need to say that the husband writes her a "new ketubah." They could have answered directly that she will waive on the condition that the ketubah remains payable upon divorce but is waived upon death. If a complete waiver is within her power, such a conditional waiver should likewise be possible and would directly explain the purchaser's loss. Moreover, writing a ketubah in an unusual conditional formulation may itself be prohibited because one should not alter the standard form fixed by the Sages. We are therefore left, with respect to the Rosh, with the explanation cited by Knesset HaGedolah in the name of the Rashach: if a debtor writes in a promissory note that he obligates himself to the creditor personally but not to that creditor's creditors, the condition is valid because a stipulation concerning monetary rights is effective. The husband can therefore write the replacement ketubah after the waiver with an express condition that the obligation is to the wife but not to her creditors. The rabbinic purpose of the ketubah remains fully intact, because divorce is no easier in his eyes and he still owes her the entire ketubah upon divorce. Yet the replacement debt does not become directly encumbered to her creditor under Rabbi Natan's rule because the husband expressly excluded that derivative right. After the husband's death she can waive the ketubah to his heirs, and Rabbi Natan does not interfere because the very terms of the replacement obligation excluded her creditors. It follows that the Ramban and Ran's central rule is confirmed even from Tosafot and the Rosh: where Rabbi Natan's rule actually applies, the intermediate creditor cannot waive the ultimate debtor's obligation. A ketubah while the woman remains married is exceptional. According to the Ran, Rabbi Natan does not yet apply because the time for collection has not arrived and the debt is contingent. According to the Rosh as I explained him above in seif katan 1, the distinction rests on the special structure of the ketubah rather than necessarily on the Ran's exact rationale. There is, however, a practical difference concerning dowry property. According to the Ran's reasoning, even dowry may remain outside Rabbi Natan while the marriage continues, since collection is also contingent and if she dies first there may be no later collection. According to the Rosh as explained above, Rabbi Natan does apply to the dowry. Later, in siman 424, I explain that the Tur and Rama rule according to the Rosh. This is the preferable ruling, because the Ran's position is otherwise singular and was introduced only because of the particular difficulty in the ketubah sugya. We should not extend that exceptional reasoning to the dowry property that she actually brought into the marriage. It is true that in my novellae to Ketubot I found some support for the Ran from the Rosh himself. The Rosh rules that where a wife borrowed for necessary support, her lender can collect directly from the husband under Rabbi Natan's rule without a prior assessment by beit din. Yet concerning a minor wife who borrowed and did not exercise her right of refusal, the Rosh requires a judicial assessment before the husband must pay, and the Gidulei Terumah questions why. According to the Ran the distinction is understandable. In the case of the minor, Rabbi Natan does not yet apply because she can still refuse the marriage, so the husband's obligation is not fixed. It resembles a ketubah during the husband's lifetime, and therefore prior assessment is required. I discussed this there at length. The foregoing also yields a rule where Shimon's loan to Levi was made after Shimon had already borrowed from Reuven. Tosafot appears to incline toward the authorities who hold that in this temporal order Levi does not become directly obligated to Reuven under Rabbi Natan. If Shimon then waives Levi's debt, Levi can certainly say kim li that the waiver is valid. Many authorities hold even more broadly that an intermediate creditor can waive despite Rabbi Natan, and here there are additional authorities who say that Rabbi Natan never attached in the first place. Thus the possessor can combine the two independent bodies of authority, as I explained in the pamphlet concerning rules of possession. A difficulty for those authorities is how later dated promissory notes can be valid. Suppose Reuven lent to Shimon in Nisan, Shimon lent to Levi in Iyar, and the witnesses dated Reuven's note in Sivan. If Levi is not directly obligated to Reuven when his debt arose only after Reuven's original loan, then under the true chronology Shimon could waive Levi's debt. By moving Reuven's note to Sivan, however, the witnesses would make it appear that Levi's Iyar debt preceded Reuven's note and would thereby subject Levi to Rabbi Natan, preventing waiver. The witnesses would have prejudiced Levi. The answer is that those authorities can agree where Reuven's note contains an after acquired property clause. If Shimon expressly encumbered to Reuven all property and rights that he would later acquire, then a debt that arises later can become subject to Reuven notwithstanding the sequence. The temporal limitation applies only where no such clause exists. We rule that a deliberately later dated note is valid only when the appropriate after acquired property language is present. There is therefore no difficulty. From all this it is established that the Rosh holds that where Rabbi Natan's rule does apply, waiver is ineffective. The Tur therefore correctly rules here that Shimon cannot waive. Knesset HaGedolah and the Taz ask why the Tur relied on a responsum of the Rosh rather than the Rosh's ruling in Ketubot, where he appears to allow waiver. According to what I have written, there is no contradiction. The Rosh's own discussion in the chapter HaChovel supports the same conclusion, as I explained at the beginning of this siman at length. The Shach also addresses the Ramban's question, which the Maharshal raises from the law of a found receipt. How can the Gemara say that a receipt should be returned because the creditor has a migo that she could waive the underlying debt? Perhaps this woman owes money to others and therefore cannot waive under Rabbi Natan. The Shach answers that it is uncommon for someone to lend money to a married woman who is living with her husband. Apart from the intrinsic difficulty of this answer, it does not resolve the Mishnah's general case of found receipts. The Mishnah says not to return them because perhaps they were written in advance and the parties later reconsidered, but if the obligor says, "Give it," one gives it. The Gemara asks why we should not suspect collusion. One cannot simply invoke Shmuel's rule that the creditor could waive, because perhaps the creditor owes others and waiver would be ineffective under Rabbi Natan. The Shach's rarity answer does not fit the Mishnah generally. I do not wish to lengthen this further, for I have already discussed the matter at length above in siman 66 and siman 54. After all this labor and clarification, however, my mind is still not settled by the categorical conclusion that the intermediate creditor cannot waive. If I could only fully understand the principle. It is agreed above in siman 85 and later in siman 111 that if Reuven lent to Shimon and Shimon lent to Levi in a way that subjects Levi directly to Reuven under Rabbi Natan, and Shimon then sells or gives Levi's note to Yehudah, then if Yehudah collects movable property from Levi, Reuven has no claim against Yehudah. Since Levi paid in movables, we treat the matter as though the movables first reached Shimon and Shimon then sold or gave them away, and ordinary movables are not encumbered to Reuven. I explained this in siman 85 at length. Why then should Levi's position be worse if Shimon gives the note to Levi himself by forgiving his debt? If Shimon gives the note as a gift to Yehudah, Yehudah acquires it and Reuven's effective claim to the movables is lost. If Shimon instead gives the same debt to Levi himself and relinquishes collection, why should Levi have a weaker position and permit Reuven to object? Levi is the possessor of his own movables. Why should saying "it is forgiven to you" or "it is given to you" be worse than giving the right to a third party? Indeed, the entire debate whether Shimon can waive seems avoidable, because he could simply say, "I give you the debt as a gift." This is extremely difficult. See the Shach in this siman, seif katan 5, in the passage beginning "however, it appears to me," where he writes explicitly that saying a note is a trust document, paid, or forgiven cannot be weaker than giving the note away as a gift. His reasoning there is correct. Tosafot in Ketubot 81b likewise implies that a debtor's power through waiver can be stronger than through gift. Tosafot asks why the yavam cannot say, "Since I am the heir, I have taken possession," by waiving the debt to himself. Yet the Gemara states that he may not give the property away as an ordinary gift. Tosafot's question therefore presupposes that self waiver may work even where an ordinary gift is restricted. The difficulty is thus sharpened. What difference should there be between Shimon's giving the debt to a third party and giving it to Levi himself? The reason a third party can retain collected movables is that we deem them as though they first came into Shimon's possession and were then transferred by him. The same should apply to waiver. It should be as though Shimon had already collected the movables from Levi and then immediately returned them to Levi as a gift. If Levi actually paid Shimon in movables and Shimon returned those very movables to him, Reuven could not object. Why should direct waiver be different? The Rosh writes similarly in a responsum cited by the Tur at the end of this siman. Shimon may lend his money to Levi for a long term and Reuven cannot prevent him, because if Shimon wanted to give the money away as a gift, Reuven could not stop him. If so, even after Shimon has lent the money, an extension of Levi's due date or a waiver of the debt should be treated like collection followed by a gift or sale, with no greater power in Reuven to object. The Rosh himself treats an extension of time as a gift. Yet with respect to movable property it is clear that an earlier creditor cannot prevent such a gift. Why then should he be able to prevent an extension or waiver? In short, I remain astonished and do not know how to resolve it. My eyes await Hashem to illuminate the matter. I am therefore compelled to suggest a new distinction. Quite apart from the foregoing problem, another difficulty points in the same direction. The Rosh in Bava Batra, chapter HaSefinah, writes that sale of promissory notes is rabbinic, and he connects the seller's power to waive with the rabbinic nature of the sale. In Perek Mi SheMet the Gemara likewise explains a power of waiver by reference to a rabbinic transfer. Rabbenu Tam, who holds that note sale is biblical, requires the separate theory of two obligations, the property lien and the personal obligation, with the personal obligation remaining in the seller's hands. But for the view that note sale is rabbinic, that theory is unnecessary. Waiver follows precisely because the purchaser's acquisition is only rabbinic. The Rosh's own words in HaSefinah plainly indicate that he accepts the rabbinic view, as the Tur records in his abridgment. How then could a direct Rabbi Natan obligation, which is full Torah law, be eliminated through the same waiver doctrine whose rationale is that an ordinary note purchaser has only a rabbinic acquisition? This strongly suggests that the cases must be divided according to the type of property available from the ultimate debtor. Where Levi owns land, the principal lien of his debt rests on that land, and under Rabbi Natan the land is directly encumbered to Reuven. If Shimon sells Levi's note to Yehudah and Yehudah collects land from Levi, we rule above in siman 85 that the transfer does not defeat Reuven. Reuven can recover the land from Yehudah. Therefore, in a case of waiver, we presume that collection would ordinarily have been from the land, for that is the primary property lien. Shimon cannot validly transfer that land away to defeat Reuven, whether to another person or back to Levi, and he likewise cannot waive the direct land based obligation. Levi cannot answer, "Had Shimon demanded payment I would have paid him with movables." Until payment actually occurs, the ordinary collection lien rests on the land. Tosafot in Bava Batra 76 asks why sale of notes should not be biblical because the land lien is transferable by deed and therefore should not be subject to waiver. Tosafot does not answer that the debtor might have chosen to pay movables, in which event the land lien would never have been used. Evidently such a hypothetical assertion by the debtor is insufficient. The existing lien is measured by the land that is presently encumbered. But where Levi has no land at all and possesses only movables, why should waiver not be effective? The entire practical reach of the obligation is then into movables. If Levi paid Shimon with movables, Shimon could give them to another, and certainly could return them to Levi. Waiver is no weaker than that result, as the Shach himself says. There is no existing land lien that survives transfer and that Reuven can follow. In such a case the logic for denying waiver collapses. This distinction appears to me clear and true.

Therefore, all the authorities who speak categorically of inability to waive should be understood as speaking where the ultimate debtor owns land and the first creditor possesses a lien capable of reaching it. This is especially evident in the case of the woman who caused injury, because a ketubah historically rested on land and not on movables. The same is true in the case of a found receipt in Bava Metzia, where the concern likewise presumes a collectible land lien. By contrast, in the Ketubot case of one who says that his note is a trust document, the statement is general and includes a debtor with only movables. The Rosh therefore correctly argues that the creditor has a migo of waiver or gift. His words are exact, and there is no contradiction in his rulings. The Shach questions the Rama on another point. Here the Rama follows the Mechaber and does not dissent from the rule that the intermediate creditor cannot waive. Yet in Even HaEzer siman 70 the Rama rules that if a wife borrowed for necessary support, her lender can collect from the husband under Rabbi Natan's rule, but if she waived her support claim against the husband, the lender loses. The Shach answers that the Rama means she waived before borrowing. This is strained, because then the ruling teaches very little. Moreover, the source is the Mordechai, and the Mordechai speaks of a waiver after the loan. The Mordechai follows his own view that even under Rabbi Natan's rule the middle creditor can waive, as the Beit Shmuel notes. The Beit Shmuel's alternative, that the wife has independent property from which the lender can collect, is likewise difficult. One possibility is that the wife borrowed in advance for support covering several future months and then immediately waived her claim to future support before those months arrived. The husband's support obligation does not arise as one fixed debt for all future months. It accrues day by day. Rabbi Natan therefore does not presently create a direct lien for support that has not yet accrued. The waiver can consequently be effective as to those future amounts. A better answer is that the Rama distinguishes between a full Torah level Rabbi Natan obligation and a support obligation whose source is rabbinic. Where Rabbi Natan operates upon an underlying Torah debt, the resulting direct lien has Torah force and cannot be waived in the manner of an ordinary sold note. But the husband's support obligation is rabbinic. The lender's derivative right is therefore no stronger than that rabbinic obligation, and waiver can operate much as it does with an ordinary sale of a note whose acquisition is rabbinic. I discussed this at length in my novellae to Even HaEzer, and this is not the place to expand further.

And if after he became obligated, etc. The Shach concludes that the wording "after he became obligated" is not literal. Rather, even if the first creditor merely warned the ultimate debtor, "Do not pay so and so, because he owes me and you are directly obligated to me under Rabbi Natan's rule," and the ultimate debtor nevertheless paid the middle creditor on his own initiative, he must pay the first creditor as well. The Shach's reasoning is persuasive. At first glance, however, one might infer otherwise from Bava Kamma, in the chapter concerning an ox that gored four or five times, where the Gemara speaks specifically of a case in which beit din first seized the ox. It does not say that the injured party himself seized it. This seems to imply that Rabbi Natan's direct lien requires formal judicial action. If the injured party himself seized the ox, the owner could then say, "You should have returned it to me," and the injured party could not answer that he was directly entitled to it under Rabbi Natan. The Gemara therefore had to say that beit din seized it, because only then does Rabbi Natan's rule become effective. Nevertheless, logic supports the Shach. The direct obligation arises already at the time of the underlying loan, as indicated by the verse "to the one to whom he is guilty." Beit din does not create the lien. Its function is only to adjudicate and enforce what already exists. I already explained above in seif katan 5 why the Gemara specifically described judicial seizure. It is true that the Mordechai in the second chapter of Dayanei Gezeirot writes that if, after the wife sued the depositary in beit din, the depositary returned the property to the husband, he must pay her. That language implies that a prior suit in beit din is necessary. The Ran also appears to require a judicial demand. Even more strongly, the Rosh's responsum concerning a recalcitrant debtor, which the Mechaber cites in this seif, states explicitly that the third party must pay because beit din ordered him not to return the property to the recalcitrant debtor. The Rosh explains that the judicial order is as though beit din had already collected the property for the creditor, thereby divesting the recalcitrant debtor of his control. This appears directly contrary to the Shach. The answer is that the Mordechai follows his own view that the intermediate creditor can waive a Rabbi Natan claim. Likewise, this responsum of the Rosh reflects the view he held before retracting that position, or, according to what I wrote above, concerns movable property, where everyone may agree that waiver can work. If waiver is effective, then ordinary voluntary payment by the ultimate debtor to the middle creditor is no better than a waiver. The first creditor therefore needs the additional fact that beit din expressly prohibited payment and effectively collected the property for him. Once judicial seizure has occurred, the middle creditor no longer has power to defeat it. But according to our accepted ruling that the middle creditor cannot waive a valid Rabbi Natan lien, there is no distinction between waiver and payment. The ultimate debtor is already directly obligated to the first creditor, and no additional act of beit din is needed to create that obligation. This is clear and also explains the Rosh's responsum according to the view there that waiver was effective. One should not try to use the explanation I gave above concerning the Rosh in Bava Kamma, namely that he may have held that Rabbi Natan prevents waiver. That source is not decisive here, because where payment rather than waiver is involved beit din could issue an order and thereby effect a judicial collection, while with a pure waiver beit din cannot simply confiscate the creditor's own property right in the same manner. Consider this carefully.

segments.he: לפיכך אפילו יש עדים וכו' הקשה הש"ך דלקמן בסי' ת' בשני שורים נוגחים והניזק אמר גדול הזיקו והמזיק אמר קטן הזיק דמדמי ליה הגמ' בס"פ המניח לטען בחיטין והודה בשעורים דפטור פסק המחבר כרמב"ם דאם יש עדים על הנגיחה הרי זה משתלם מן הקטן וביקש הש"ך לחלק דמ"ש כאן אפי' יש עדים היינו שמעידים בבירור על שעורים אבל לקמן מיירי שראו נגיחה ולא ידעו מי נגח ואף כאן ביודעים הלואה וא"י אם חיטין או שעורים חייב בשעורים דהוא יאמר בממ"נ אם האמת כדברי העדים תן לי עכ"פ שעורים עכ"ל. ובלבד דקשה דא"כ איך השמיט המחבר הך דינא במעידים הלואה סתם דנוטל עכ"פ שעורים אלא דלא הבנתי הטעם מה בממ"נ יש אם העידו על חיטין תן לי חיטין ואם על שעורים תן לי שעורים הא במעידים להדי' על שעורים לית לה שעורים ומ"ש דאומרי' דרך ספק או דרך החלט סוף כל סוף הא אם אמת דשעורים היה הודה ומחל לו ואיך יוציא ממון מספק ובפרט כפי שמשמע מדברי הגמרא שם וכמ"ש לקמן בישוב דברי רמב"ם במזיק אומר שמא וניזק ברי ה"ל טענו בחיטין וכו' ומ"ש הודאת פיו ומ"ש עדים הא הודאת בע"ד עדיף ממאה עדים ולכן לא הבנתי על בוריו טעם לחלק. ומה שנראה דברמב"ם גופי' יש לדקדק דלא זו שלא הזכיר דין זה ביש עדים דמשלם הפחות בהל' טוען ונטען גבי טוען בחיטין וכו' אף גם שם בהל' נזקי ממון הביאו באמצע פסקה מל הך בבא דשנים רודפים אחד גדול וא' קטן דאם יש עדים ולא הביאו לבסוף אחרי כל הבבית השנוים במשנה אחד תם ואחד מועד ושנים רודפים אחר שנים דהא לכאורה הך דינא מישך שייכי לכל הבבית כמ"ש המ"מ. ולכן נראה דבכוונה שמר הסדר דצריך טעם מה יועיל עדים יותר מהודאות עצמו דהודה בקטו או בשעורים ומ"מ פטור וא"כ מה יועיל עדים ונראה הטעם דס"ל לרמב"ם בתפס לא נפטר משעורים וקי"ל כר"ע דאמר שותפים נינהו ואם הקדישו ניזק הוי הקדש דהרי הוא שלו וא"כ צ"ל דהוי החצי כאלו בא בידו ואיך שייך בו מחילה דמחילה שייך על תביעה על חבירו אבל על מה שהוא שלו לא יתכן ולא מהני לשון מחילה רק צ"ל להדי' בלשון מתנה נתון לך וזה אינו בל' בתבעו גדול שיהיה כאומר נתון לך הקטן וכיון דהוא ברשותו לא שייך ביה דין טענו בחיטין והודה בשעורים ועדיף מתפוס אך הני מילי בשכבר הודה לו בו המזיק או יש עדים א"כ הרי בידו להביאו כל שעה ולמוכרו ולכך חצי השור מוחלט לו. וכמ"ש תו' בריש שור שנגח ד' וה' ד"ה שור וכו' דהואיל דיש בידו להביא עדים לאלתר זכה בשמירתו ע"ש. אבל כל כמה דאין לו עדים ועדיין לא הודה הנתבע א"כ איך יהיה השור מוחלט לו הא עדיין יכול המזיק לכפור בו ולומר לא כי בסלע לקה וכדומה או א"י וא"כ פשיטא דאז עדיין בתכלית הראוי ולא מיקרי כלל גבי' ואין עדיין מוחלט לו ולכך אמרינן בגמרא תבעו בגדול והודה בקטן דה"ל כטען בחיטי' והודה בשעורים דאז בעת תביעתו בגדול עדיין לא הודה המזיק כלל ומחוסר גוביינא ואז בתביעתו מחל למזיק הקטן דעדיין ברשותו דמזיק קאי וא"כ מה יועיל שאח"כ מודה המזיק בקטן כבר נמחל לו וא"ש: (ובגמ' לא איירי ביש עדים על הנגיחה דסוגיא אתיא למ"ד פ"נ ממונא וכמ"ש המחברים ופשוט) משא"כ ביש עדים על נגיחה לא מבעיא דמעידים על הקטן אלא אפי' מעידים בספיקא מ"מ קאי הקטן ברשותו דמספיקא אין לו רק הקטן וה"ל כמעידים רק על הקטן וכ"כ הרא"ש באומר יודע אני שהיה המשכון שוה יותר מסלע וא"י כמה דה"ל כמודה בדבר שבמנין דכיון דהודה סתם ה"ל כמודה בפרוטה דתפסתה מרובה וכו' ומכ"ש בזה במעידים בספק אין ברשותו אלא הקטן וזהו ודאי ברשותו ויכול להביאו כל עת ושותף הוא בו ולא שייך מחילה כלל. ועיין לקמן ס"ק י"ד במ"ש בשם בעה"ת דכתב לדעת הרמב"ם דפקדון יותר מיקרי חיוב לגבי נפקד משור תם לגבי מזיק ולכך לא הוי הוד' ממין טענה כלל דאין על המזיק שום חיוב. ולכך העמיד הרמב"ם דבריו על הך בבא בשני תמים רודפים וכו' משא"כ אלו כתבו לבסוף באחד תם וא' מועד והמזיק אומר מועד הזיק הקטן ודאי דמ"מ אין לניזק דמי קטן דהא מחלו באומרו שהזיק לגדול וגבי מועד ליכא תפיסה ואינו מוחלט לו כלל דהא מעלי' משתלם ואינו רק ב"ח בעלמא על המזיק ואלו כתבו לבסוף אף על זה היה מוסב וזה שקר ולכך הקדימו וכתבו במקום הראוי ולהציל המעיין מטעות. ומכ"ש דלא שייך הך דינא בטענו שהלוהו חיטין ומודה בשעורים והעדים מעידים בשעורים או שאינם יודעים באיזה מין היתה הלואה דכאן לא שייך מ"ש וה"ל כמועד דהא אין לו רק חיוב על הלוה ולא מיקרי תפי' כלל ופשוט ולכך לא עשה מיניה כלל זכר בהלכות טוען ונטען. וגם דברי מחבר יפה מתפרשין. ובאמת אפשר בטען חיטין פקדון והודה בשעורים פקדון ועדים מעידים בשעורים או שא"י מהו ויודעים שלא קרהו אסון באופן דא"א לטעון נאנסו וא"כ שעורים לא מחוסר גוביינא וכל היכי דאיתא ברשותו דמפקיד קאי באמת לא שייך ביה מחילה ודין דטען בחיטין והודה בשעורים והבו דלא לוסיף דבלא"ה הרבה מחברים ס"ל כל הטעם השטאה דלא מהני בעדים והיינו באופנים הנזכרים באופן שלא יכול לכפור כלל מיהו כבר כתבתי דתם גרע מפקדון כמ"ש בעה"ת. ונראה דיש לרמב"ם ראיה מהא דאמרי' בגמרא ואי לא מייתי ראיה שקול כדאמר מזיק ואמאי הא ה"ל טענו בחיטין וכו' ומשני הגמרא ראוי ליטול ואין לו. וכבר הקשו התו' דהל"ל פטור ותי' התוספת דנתכוון לתי' השני דתפס לא ס"ל לרמב"ם. ולכך פי' הרמב"ם דכך פי' במשנה הממע"ה כל מה שירצה להוציא צריך ראיה דלא מבעיא כשירצה להוציא כטענתו דמי גדול פשיטא דצריך ראיה אלא אפי' שירצה להוציא דמי קטן דאמר מזיק דזהו שורת הדין לכאורה ראוי ליטול מ"מ אין לו עד שיביא ראיה וכללא הוא לכל מה שירצה להוציא הן רב או מעט צריך ראיה דזולת זה ה"ל כטען בחיטין וכו' מיהו בראיה שקול וזהו מבואר כדברי הרמב"ם דביש עדים שקול כדאמר מזיק וא"כ טובא קמ"ל המשנה בהך הממע"ה ביש עדים דשקיל כדאמר מזיק וא"א למתני פטור דהוי משמע אפילו יש עדים על הנגיחה וא"ש ומדויק. והנה הרב הש"ך האריך בזה בס"ק ט"ז דלא זו ביש עדים דמוציאין שעורים אף גם בעומד בהודאתו דחייב שעורים חייב לשלם דכל טעמו דפטרינן משעורים הוא כדעת הראב"ד ורמ"ה דיכול הנתבע לטעון משטה הייתי בך הואיל ותבעת דבר שאינו ואף שהוא בב"ד אבל במודה דחייב ולא השטה פשיטא דחייב ועם כל אריכות שלו לא מצאתי בכל דבריו דבר ברור שכדאי להכריע נגד גדולי חקרי לבב ההמה החולקים כי עיקר דבריו כי סוגי' דגמ' אזלא למ"ד פ"נ ממון או דמיירי בטענו גדול הזיק וכבר העמדתיך בדין ונתחייבת לי דמי גדול והוא אומר לא כי רק דמי קטן ואמת דכן כתבו המחברים דמיירי למ"ד פ"נ ממון (ומ"ש הש"ך דמיירי בהעמיד בדין עיין מש"ל בזה) אך עם כל זה קשה לומר דפי' המשנה יהיה והלה אומר קטן הזיק ועכשיו חוזר מדבריו ואמר להשטות נתכוונתי ואף אנו היינו צריכין לפרש כן ליישב המשנה בזה היה ק' לומר כן דמשנה סתמא קתני והלה אומר משמע דאומר ובא ולא קתני היה אומר מכ"ש דקשה מנ"ל לגמרא לעשות מיניה קושיא ולומר דמיירי בדתפס וכיוצא. מה דלא מצינו רמז ממנו במשנה ולא מוקי ליה בפשוט דעומד בדיבורו ואינו חוזר בו ואין כוונת המשנה בזה רק מי הזיק קטן או גדול אבל לא נחית לומר דחוזר ואומר דלא הזיק כלל דהא שור מנוגח לפניך ומה תאמר בסלע לקה היינו רישא ומה קמ"ל בסיפא. ולא מצאתי לרמ"ה רמז בשמעת' רק מהא דמשני ראוי ליטול ואין לו דנדחקו התו' בפירושו וצ"ל דמוסב על הך תי' שני בדתפס ולפי' רמ"ה א"ש ראוי ליטול אם עומד המזיק בדיבורו ואין לו אם יחזור בו ויאמר להשטות כוונתי. וטובא קמ"ל דהטעם משום השטאה ופעמים יש לו ופעמים אין לו. אך אף דזה נכון מיני' תברא דקשי' לרמ"ה א"כ מה דוחקיה דגמרא לומר במציעתא דשם מיירי בניזק אומר שמא מזיק ברי ולא משני הך תי' ראוי ליטול ואין לו ועל מציעתא לא קשה מברייתא הרי זה משתלם דבמציעתא לא נאמרה ברייתא (וכמו דצ"ל לפי' רש"י דהקשו דהל"ל במציעתא ראוי ליטול וכו' וע"כ אין כוונתו על תפס דא"כ יקשה תרתי ל"ל אלא ס"ל ראוי ליטול אינו מוסב על תפוס כמו שנראה מפירש"י להדיא רק בפשוט ולכך הקושיא במיצעתא דליכא ברייתא לוקמי בראוי ליטול וסיפא דאיכא ברייתא דקתני להדיא דמשתלם לוקי בדתפס) וסיפא דקתני ברייתא לוקמי בדתפס ותרווייהו צריכי דקמ"ל בדתפס אפי' אינו עומד בדיבורו לא מהני וחייב וגם קמ"ל בדלא תפס ועומד בדבורו דג"כ חייב ול"ל דקים ליה לגמרא דאף על מציעת' יש ברייתא דמשלם מקטן מ"מ ה"ל לגמ' לאתויא זה בקשיא דהקשה לימא תיובתא דרב"נ הל"ל דקשיא מברייתא דהא במשנה י"ל ראוי ליטול וכן צ"ל בכוונת רש"י כמש"ל דאל"כ גם רש"י לא הקשה מידי. ול"ל דס"ל לרמ"ה כתי' רש"י דהואיל דס"ל לא אמר סומכוס אפי' ברי וברי א"כ ניחא ליה לאוקמי מציעת' בניז' אומר שמא דעדיין קשה א"כ מה פריך ר"פ למ"ד דאמר סומכוס אפי' ברי וברי מהך מציעת' הא לדידי' שפיר י"ל דגם מציעתא איירי ברי וברי רק ראוי ליטול ואין לו.
segments.en: Therefore , even if there are witnesses, etc. The Shach asks from the ruling below in siman 400 concerning two oxen that gored, where the injured party says that the larger ox caused the damage and the owner says that the smaller ox caused it. The Gemara at the end of chapter HaManiach compares this to one who claimed wheat and the other admitted barley, where he is exempt. Yet the Mechaber rules, following Rambam, that if there are witnesses to the goring, the injured party collects from the smaller ox. The Shach seeks to distinguish between the cases. What is stated here, that even if there are witnesses he is exempt, means that they testify clearly concerning barley. Below, however, the witnesses saw a goring but did not know which ox gored. So too here, if they know that there was a loan but do not know whether it was wheat or barley, the claimant should at least recover the value of the barley, because he can say: whichever way you look at it, if the witnesses are telling the truth, give me at least the barley. These are his words. This is difficult, however, for if so, why did the Mechaber omit the rule that where witnesses testify merely that there was a loan, the claimant at least recovers the barley? More fundamentally, I do not understand the reasoning. What sort of whichever way you look at it argument is there? If the witnesses testified to wheat, give him wheat, and if they testified to barley, give him barley. But where they testify explicitly to barley, the claimant has no right to the barley. What difference is there whether they speak doubtfully or decisively? In the end, if the truth is that the debt was barley, then by claiming wheat he admitted and waived the barley. How can money be extracted because of a doubt? This is particularly difficult in light of what appears from the Gemara there, and as I will write below in explaining Rambam, that where the tortfeasor says he is uncertain and the injured party makes a definite claim, it is treated as one who claimed wheat, etc. What difference is there between an admission by his own mouth and testimony of witnesses? An admission by a litigant is stronger than one hundred witnesses. I therefore do not fully understand the basis for this distinction. There is also a precision to be noted in Rambam himself. Not only did he fail to mention in Hilchot To'en VeNitan, in the discussion of one who claims wheat and the other admits barley, the rule that where witnesses exist he pays the lesser amount, but even in Hilchot Nizkei Mamon he inserted this rule in the middle of the paragraph dealing with two pursuing oxen, one large and one small, saying that if there are witnesses, etc. He did not place it at the end after all the cases taught in the Mishnah, namely one tam and one mu'ad, and two oxen pursuing two others. Seemingly this rule should apply to all the cases, as the Maggid Mishneh writes. It therefore appears that Rambam deliberately preserved this order, because one must explain why witnesses should help more than the defendant's own admission. He himself admitted that the smaller ox caused the damage, or that he owed barley, yet he is nevertheless exempt. What, then, do witnesses add? It appears that the reason is that Rambam holds that where the injured party seized the lesser amount he is not deprived of it, and we rule like Rabbi Akiva, who says that the injured party and the owner are partners in the offending ox. If the injured party consecrated his share it is consecrated, because it is already his. It follows that his half share is regarded as though it had come into his possession. How can waiver apply to something that is already his? Waiver applies to a claim against another person, but not to property that belongs to the claimant himself. With respect to property that is already his, the language of waiver is ineffective. One would have to say explicitly, in the language of a gift, that it is given to the other party. A claim that the larger ox caused the damage cannot be interpreted as saying, "The smaller ox is given to you." Since his portion of the smaller ox is already deemed in his possession, the rule of claiming wheat and admitting barley does not apply. This is even stronger than an actual seizure. This is true, however, only once the tortfeasor has already admitted the matter or witnesses exist. At that point the injured party can bring the ox at any time and sell it, and therefore half the ox is conclusively his. Tosafot likewise write at the beginning of the chapter Shor Shenagach Arba'ah VaChamishah, s.v. shor, that because the injured party has the ability to bring witnesses immediately, he acquires rights in the ox with respect to its safeguarding. See there. But as long as he has no witnesses and the defendant has not yet admitted anything, how can the ox be conclusively his? The owner can still deny liability and say, for example, that the injured ox was struck by a rock, or say that he does not know. In such a case the injured party is certainly still lacking collection, and the ox is not considered in his possession at all. It is not yet conclusively his. Therefore, when the Gemara speaks of a claimant who says the large ox caused the damage and the owner admits that the small ox did, this means that when the claimant first asserted his claim regarding the large ox, the tortfeasor had not yet admitted anything and collection was still lacking. At that moment, by asserting only the claim concerning the large ox, he waived the claim against the smaller ox, which was still entirely in the tortfeasor's possession. Once it was already waived, the owner's subsequent admission concerning the smaller ox cannot restore it. This is properly explained. The Gemara there does not deal with witnesses to the goring, because that discussion follows the opinion that half damages are compensatory rather than a fine, as the authorities explain, and this is straightforward. By contrast, where witnesses testify to the goring, it makes no difference whether they testify specifically about the smaller ox or testify only that one of the oxen gored. In either case the injured party's rights attach to the smaller ox, because in a case of doubt he can recover no more than from the smaller ox. It is therefore equivalent to testimony specifically concerning the smaller ox. The Rosh similarly writes regarding one who says, "I know that the pledge was worth more than a sela, but I do not know how much more," that this is regarded as an admission of a quantified amount, because an unspecified admission is treated as an admission of a perutah, under the principle that where grasping the larger amount would be excessive, one grasps the smaller amount. All the more so here, where the witnesses testify doubtfully, the injured party has no established right except in the smaller ox. That smaller ox, however, is certainly within his legal possession. He can bring it for collection at any time and is a partner in it, so waiver cannot apply to it at all. See below, seif katan 14, where I cite the Baal HaTerumot as explaining Rambam's view that a deposit creates a stronger obligation upon the bailee than a tam ox creates upon the tortfeasor. Therefore, in the case of a tam ox, the owner's admission is not considered an admission of the same kind as the claim at all, because the tortfeasor has no personal monetary obligation. For this reason Rambam stated his ruling specifically in the case of two tam oxen pursuing, etc. Had he placed the ruling at the end, after the case of one tam and one mu'ad, it would have appeared to apply also where the owner says that the mu'ad, smaller ox caused the damage. In that case the injured party certainly would not collect the value of the smaller ox, because by claiming that the larger ox caused the damage he waived that lesser claim. With a mu'ad ox there is no proprietary seizure and no share of the ox is conclusively the injured party's, since payment comes from the owner's superior assets. The injured party is merely an ordinary creditor of the tortfeasor. Had Rambam placed the rule at the end, it would have appeared to apply to this case as well, which would be incorrect. He therefore advanced the ruling to its proper place in order to prevent the reader from making this mistake. All the more so, this rule cannot apply where the claimant says that he lent wheat and the defendant admits barley, while witnesses testify to barley or merely testify that there was a loan without knowing which commodity was lent. In such a case none of the reasoning just stated applies. It is comparable to the case of a mu'ad ox, because the claimant has only a personal claim against the borrower and nothing is regarded as already seized or conclusively his. This is straightforward, and therefore Rambam made no mention of such a rule in Hilchot To'en VeNitan. The Mechaber's words are likewise readily explained in this manner. It is indeed possible that if the claimant says that wheat was deposited and the defendant admits a deposit of barley, and witnesses testify concerning barley or testify to the deposit without knowing which commodity it was, while also knowing that no mishap occurred so that the bailee cannot claim that the property was lost through an unavoidable accident, then the barley is not lacking collection. Wherever the deposit is, it stands in the depositor's legal possession. In that circumstance waiver truly should not apply, nor should the ordinary rule of claiming wheat and admitting barley. We should not extend the exemption beyond its established scope. Quite apart from this, many authorities hold that the entire basis for the exemption is that the defendant may say that his admission was made merely to mock the claimant, and that reasoning does not apply when witnesses exist, namely in the circumstances described where he cannot deny the matter at all. Nevertheless, I have already written that a tam ox is weaker than a deposit, as the Baal HaTerumot states. It appears that Rambam has a proof from the Gemara. The Gemara says: if the injured party does not bring proof, he takes according to what the tortfeasor says. It then asks why, since this should be a case of claiming wheat and admitting barley. The Gemara answers that he is fit to take, but in fact has nothing. Tosafot already ask why the Mishnah did not simply say that he is exempt, and they answer according to their second resolution concerning seizure, which Rambam does not accept. Rambam therefore explains the Mishnah as follows. The principle that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant means that for anything he wishes to extract, he must bring proof. It is obvious that if he seeks to collect according to his own claim, namely the value of the larger ox, he must bring proof. The Mishnah adds that even if he seeks to collect only the value of the smaller ox, which the tortfeasor himself says is the amount due and which would seemingly be recoverable as a matter of law, he still has nothing until he brings proof. For every amount that he seeks to extract, large or small, he needs proof. Without such proof, it is a case of claiming wheat and admitting barley. Once he brings proof, however, he collects according to what the tortfeasor says. This is precisely Rambam's ruling that where witnesses exist he collects according to the tortfeasor's admission. The Mishnah therefore teaches a substantial point through the phrase that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant. It tells us that with witnesses he collects according to what the tortfeasor says. It could not simply teach "exempt," because that would imply exemption even where witnesses testify to the goring. Everything is thus properly explained and precise. The Shach, in seif katan 16, discusses this at length and holds that not only where witnesses exist can the barley be recovered, but even where the defendant remains by his admission and continues to acknowledge that he owes the barley, he must pay it. In his view, the entire reason that one who admits barley after being sued for wheat is exempt from the barley is the view of the Raavad and Ramah, that the defendant may say: "I was mocking you because you sued me for something I do not owe." Although the admission was made in beit din, it can still be explained that way. But if the defendant acknowledges that he truly owes the barley and does not claim that he was mocking, then he certainly must pay. Despite the Shach's lengthy discussion, I have not found in his words a decisive argument sufficient to rule against the great and profound authorities who disagree. His principal point is that the Gemara's discussion follows the opinion that half damages are compensatory, or alternatively that the case is where the injured party says, "The large ox caused the damage, and you have already stood with me in judgment and become liable to me for the value of the large ox," while the owner responds, "No, only the value of the smaller ox." It is true that the authorities write that the discussion follows the opinion that half damages are compensatory. As for what the Shach writes about a prior judgment, see what I wrote above. Even so, it is difficult to say that the Mishnah's statement, "the other says that the smaller ox caused the damage," means that he is now retracting what he said and claims that he intended merely to mock the injured party. Even if we ourselves needed to explain the Mishnah this way, the interpretation would be difficult, because the Mishnah states simply that the other party "says," which implies his present and continuing position. It does not say that he "had said" this earlier. All the more so, how could the Gemara derive a difficulty from the Mishnah and then force the case into a situation of seizure or the like, when there is no indication of that in the Mishnah, rather than explain it simply as a case where the tortfeasor stands by his statement and does not retract? The Mishnah is concerned only with which ox caused the damage, the smaller or the larger, not with a later retraction in which the tortfeasor claims that his ox caused no damage at all. After all, the injured ox lies before us. If one answers that perhaps it was struck by a rock, that possibility is already the subject of the first clause, so what would the latter clause add? I have found no indication for the Ramah's explanation in the sugya except the Gemara's answer that the injured party is fit to take but in fact has nothing, an expression that Tosafot found difficult. According to the Ramah it can indeed be explained well: he is fit to collect if the tortfeasor stands by his statement, but he has nothing if the tortfeasor retracts and says that his earlier admission was intended merely to mock him. The Mishnah thereby teaches something significant, namely that the reason is the possibility of mockery, so at times he collects and at times he does not. Although this explanation is attractive, it contains its own refutation. According to the Ramah, why did the Gemara feel forced, in the middle clause, to explain the case as one in which the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor is certain? Why did it not give the same answer that the injured party is fit to take but has nothing? The baraita stating that he collects from the smaller ox was not cited concerning the middle clause. This is similar to the difficulty that must be raised according to Rashi, who asks why the Gemara did not say in the middle clause that he is fit to take, etc. It necessarily follows that Rashi does not understand "fit to take" as referring to seizure. Otherwise there would be two separate questions. Rather, he understands the phrase in its simple sense. The question regarding the middle clause is therefore that, since no baraita contradicts it, the Gemara should have explained it by saying that he is fit to take. As for the last clause, where the baraita explicitly says that he collects, the Gemara could have explained it as a case of seizure. Likewise, according to the Ramah, the Gemara could have explained the middle clause as a case where the owner stands by his admission and therefore he pays, while the last clause, in light of the baraita, could be a case of seizure. Both rulings would then be necessary. The latter would teach that even if the tortfeasor does not stand by his statement, seizure is effective, while the former would teach that even without seizure, if he stands by his statement, he must pay. One cannot answer that the Gemara knew of a baraita concerning the middle clause as well, saying that he pays from the smaller ox. Had that been so, when the Gemara sought to challenge Rav Nachman it should have cited that baraita explicitly. From the Mishnah itself there would be no difficulty, since it could be explained that he is merely fit to take. This is necessarily Rashi's intent, as explained above, for otherwise Rashi's question would have no force either. Nor can one say that the Ramah follows Rashi's answer that, since he holds that Sumchus did not state his rule where both parties make definite claims, it was preferable to explain the middle clause as a case where the injured party is uncertain. The difficulty would remain: why, according to Rav Pappa, who holds that Sumchus applies even where both parties are certain, does Rav Pappa challenge from the middle clause? According to him, the middle clause could indeed involve two definite claims, while the injured party is merely fit to collect but in fact has nothing.

segments.he: ואמת דקושי' זו קשה לרש"י ג"כ וצ"ע לכאורה רק ברש"י הרב' דרכי' יש כמ"ש בחדושי ואחד מהן דס"ל לרש"י דלכך קתני הממע"ה ולא פטור כמש"ל ברמב"ם דקמ"ל ביש עדים דנוטל והטעם כר"ע דשותפי נינהו אך קשה לכאורה א"א לומר דמתני' ר"ע היא דרש"י ס"ל כופר בכל בפקדון חייב שבועה וא"כ לר"ע דשותף נינהו ואם הקדישו קדוש ה"ל כאלו יש ביד מזיק פקדון וא"כ רישא דמוקי ליה בברי וברי והלה אומר בסלע לקה יש כאן חיוב ש"ד ואיך קמ"ל לאפוקי מדסומכס הא ה"ל חיוב ש"ד ומודה סומכס במקום שיש ש"ד כדאמרינן בב"מ בשמעת' דהמחליף דף ק' ע"ש. ועכצ"ל דר"י היא דלא ס"ל שותפי רק ב"ח ואין כאן פקדון וליכא ש"ד (ואף דהך היו שניהם של איש אחד משמע בגמרא דר"ע היא מ"מ י"ל דאידך משנה ר"י היא או באמת ס"ל ר"י היא וכן צ"ל בתו' לקמן ריש פ' הפרה דהקשו לוקמי משנ' כסומכס ור"י היא ש"מ דמצי להיות כר"י) אך י"ל דהא המהרש"א הק' בר"פ הפרה במשנה דקתני והלה אומר לא כי בסלע לקה דס"ל לחכמים הממע"ה הא אף אלו מודה מפטר למ"ד פ"נ קנסא דהא ה"ל מודה בקצת ולסומכס נמי אמאי יחלוקו וע"ש שביקש לומר דין חדש נגד הרא"ש ומחברים אבל באמת נר' לסומכס ל"ק דלמ"ד אמר סומכס אפי' ברי וברי בכה"ג דאיכא דררא דממון כמ"ש התו' א"כ ודאי במודה המזיק ואומר ששורו נגחו דפטור מרביע נזק דאלו לא הוד' היה הדין יחלוקו ובהודאתו מגיע ח"נ וה"ל מודה בקנס אבל רביע נזק חייב דהא אף דהיה מכחיש הוה הדין יחלוקו לסומכס דס"ל אפי' בברי וברי וא"כ מה אהני הודאתו אלא אפי' נימא דבברי וברי לא אמר סומכס וא"כ לכאור' י"ל הא הוי מודה בקנס דאלו לא הוד' וכפר הוי פטור מכל הנזק לסומכס אך באמת אינו דכי אמרי' מודה בקנס פטור היינו היכי דאלו שתק היה פטור רק באמירת פיו מתחייב בזו אמרי' מודה בקנס פטור. אבל אם שתק היה מתחייב דה"ל שמא ויחלוקו לסומכס רק דאנן אמרי' דהוי מצי לשקר זהו אינו בגדר מודה בקנס דיפטור הואיל ולא משק' ח"ו רק אנו אומרים אלו שתק היה פטור ובעקימת שפתיו לא יתחייב אבל במקום דשתק פטור לא אמרי' וזה פשוט ונכון. וא"כ כיון דלסומכס ברביע נזק לא מועיל מודה בקנס שפיר איצטריך לחכמים דקמ"ל הממע"ה לאפוקי מדסומכס דס"ל שקיל רביע נזק עכ"פ וקמ"ל דלא נטיל כלום ובאמת לחכמים אף במודה אינו נוטל כלום דה"ל מודה בקנס רק קמ"ל לאפוקי מדסומכס וזה ברור ונכון בישוב קו' מהרש"א ומעתה הקושי' מעיקרא ליתא דמודה סומכס בש"ד דכי יש ש"ד היינו היכי דבהודאתו מתחייב ובכפירתו מפטר רמי' שבוע' עלי' דלודה אבל כאן מה יועיל שבועתו כל מה דאינו מתחייב בלי אמירת פיו אף אמירת פיו לא מהני ומה יועיל שבוע' שלו ואין זה דומה למחליף פרה בחמור דאמרי' מודה סומכס בש"ד דשם דמתחייב הוי חיוב גמור ולק"מ. ולפ"ז נכונים דברי רש"י ומזוקקים דר"פ שפיר קפריך ממיצעת' דל"ל ראוי ליטול ביש עדים כהנ"ל וכר"ע דאמר שותפים דע"כ כר"י אתי' דאל"כ מה קמ"ל לאפוקי מסומכס הא מודה סומכס בש"ד דהוי כופר בפקדון ול"ל כהנ"ל דלא הוי ש"ד דמודה בקנס פטור דהא ר"פ ס"ל פ"נ הוא ממון ולכך מוקי ליה בניזק אומר שמא וכו' אבל קו' רש"י למסקנא דקיי"ל דהוי פ"נ קנסא ואם כן שפיר יש לומר דמשנה כר' עקיבא ואם כן קשה אסתמא דגמרא אדמקשה מסיפא לקשי ממיצעתא ולומר ראוי ליטול וכמו שכתבתי ולהוציא ממילתא דלעיל דמיירי בניז' אומר שמא ועל זה משני רש"י שפיר דלמסקנא קיי"ל לא קאמר סומכס ברי וברי ולכך מוקי ליה בכך דיהיה דומים ודוק ועיי' עוד מה שכתבתי בזה. אך כל זה אין מספיק בתי' הרמ"ה דלפי' ראוי ליטול כפשוטו אם יעמוד בדבריו כהנ"ל וקושי' הנ"ל במקומו ובפרטות דיש ראיה מתו' דנדחקו לפרש ראוי ליטול ואין לו דקאי על תפס ולא פי' כרמ"ה שמע מיניה דלא סבירא ליה כרמ"ה ודלא כש"ך דחשב דגם התו' ס"ל כרמ"ה. אך אין צורך לזה דבלא"ה דעת התו' דלא כרמ"ה כנראה לכל מעיין בדבריהם דכתבו להדיא דהוי הודא' ומחל לו ולפי' הרמ"ה מה מחילה כאן וגם איך יתכן דאף לרבה בר נתן מ"מ ס"ל כר"ג דיש כאן שבועת מ"מ ואם יכול לטעון משטה הייתי מה שבועה של מ"מ יש כאן וכמו כן הדבר מבואר ברמב"ם בהל' טוען דכתב דהוי כאומר מנה לך בידי והל' אומר אין לי בידך דפטור והא בזה לעולם פטור אפי' עומד בדבורו דהא הך יליף ליה מהר"ם והרא"ש בפי"נ מהא דאת מוד' דלאו אחונא את ולכך כל מה שטרח הש"ך להשיב דברי הרמב"ם לדעת רמ"ה בחנם טרח כי מהנמשל הזה מוכח דלעולם פטור וכ"כ הנושאי כליו. וא"כ מה לנו עוד להאריך כיון דרמב"ם ותו' ובעה"ת ורא"ש והטור והמחבר ומהרש"ל ורמ"א מתכוונים כאחד וכפי מ"ש ממש מוכח כן מדברי הגמ' אין לפקפק וכוותייהו קי"ל: וגם דעת הרמב"ן כן מבואר ברא"ש ב"מ בשמעתין דשאלה ושכורה דכתב דא"צ לישבע ששכור' מתה כדרכה הואיל ותבעו בשאולה ה"ל טענו בחיטין דפטור משעורים ע"ש והא התם ע"כ עומד בדיבורו דשכורה מתה כדרכה. ולכן העיקר כמ"ש בש"ע בלי פקפוק.
segments.en: In truth , this question is difficult at first glance even according to Rashi and requires study. Yet Rashi's approach has several possible explanations, as I wrote in my novellae. One of them is that Rashi holds that the Mishnah says, "the burden of proof rests upon the claimant," rather than simply "exempt," in order to teach, as I explained above according to Rambam, that where there are witnesses the injured party does recover. The reason is Rabbi Akiva's view that the parties are partners in the ox. At first glance, however, the Mishnah cannot be attributed to Rabbi Akiva. Rashi holds that one who totally denies a deposit is liable to take an oath. If, according to Rabbi Akiva, the injured party is already a partner in the offending ox and can validly consecrate his share, then the case is as though the tortfeasor holds a deposit belonging to the injured party. Accordingly, in the first clause, which the Gemara establishes as a case where both parties make definite claims and the tortfeasor says that the injured ox was struck by a rock, there would be a Torah oath. How, then, could the Mishnah be teaching a ruling against Sumchus? Sumchus agrees that his division rule does not apply where a Torah oath is required, as stated in Bava Metzia in the sugya of one who exchanges a cow, page 100. We must therefore say that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael, who does not hold that they are partners but only that the injured party is a creditor. There is then no deposit and no Torah oath. Although the Gemara appears to imply that the law concerning two oxen belonging to one person follows Rabbi Akiva, it is still possible that the other Mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael, or perhaps this very Mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael. Tosafot at the beginning of chapter HaParah also ask that the Mishnah could be established according to Sumchus and Rabbi Yishmael, showing that they too regard attribution to Rabbi Yishmael as possible. Yet one may answer differently. The Maharsha asks at the beginning of chapter HaParah regarding the Mishnah where the claimant says that the defendant's ox caused the damage and the defendant says that the injured animal was struck by a rock. According to the Sages, the burden of proof rests upon the claimant. But according to the opinion that half damages are a fine, even if the owner admitted that his ox caused the damage he would be exempt, because he would be one who admits liability for a fine. Why then, according to Sumchus, should they divide? See there, where the Maharsha seeks to establish a novel rule contrary to the Rosh and the other authorities. In truth, however, there is no difficulty according to Sumchus. According to the opinion that Sumchus applies even to two definite claims where there is an inherent monetary doubt, as Tosafot write, then if the tortfeasor admits that his ox gored, his admission exempts him from one quarter of the damage that otherwise would have been payable as half of the disputed half damages. Had he not admitted anything, the rule according to Sumchus would have been to divide, which would yield one quarter damages. His admission could create liability for up to half damages, but as an admission to a fine it cannot create that additional liability. Still, he must pay the quarter that would have been payable even without his admission, because that amount does not arise from his admission at all. Even if we say that Sumchus does not apply where both parties make definite claims, so that one might argue that this is an admission to a fine because had the tortfeasor denied everything he would have been exempt from all damages, the argument is still incorrect. The rule that one who admits a fine is exempt applies where, had he remained silent, he would have been exempt, and only his own words create the liability. In such a case we say that his admission cannot create the fine. But if his silence would itself have exposed him to liability, as where his silence would make him an uncertain litigant and Sumchus would require division, the fact that he could have lied and denied the claim does not convert his truthful statement into an exempting admission to a fine. We say only that where silence itself leaves him exempt, the movement of his lips cannot create the fine. Where silence would not leave him exempt, this principle does not apply. This is straightforward and correct. Accordingly, the Sages indeed need the Mishnah's rule that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant in order to reject Sumchus. Sumchus would require payment of at least one quarter of the damage, whereas the Sages teach that the claimant collects nothing. It is true that according to the Sages, even an admission by the tortfeasor would not obligate him, because it would be an admission to a fine. Nevertheless, the Mishnah states the rule in order to exclude Sumchus, according to whom the claimant would recover one quarter. This is a clear and correct resolution of the Maharsha's difficulty. We may now return to the original difficulty. Sumchus agrees that his rule does not apply where there is a Torah oath. But a Torah oath exists only where the defendant's admission actually creates the monetary obligation while his denial would exempt him, and therefore an oath is imposed upon him so that he should admit the truth. Here, however, his statement cannot itself create liability for the fine, because an admission to a fine is exempt. What purpose would the oath serve? Whatever amount cannot be imposed without his own statement cannot be imposed through his statement either. His oath therefore accomplishes nothing. This is not comparable to the case of one who exchanges a cow for a donkey, where we say that Sumchus agrees in the presence of a Torah oath, because there the defendant's admission creates a full monetary obligation. There is therefore no difficulty. According to this, Rashi's words are precise and refined. Rav Pappa properly challenges from the middle clause. The explanation that the injured party is merely fit to take where witnesses exist, according to Rabbi Akiva's partnership theory, cannot be used there, because Rav Pappa holds that half damages are compensatory. If the Mishnah followed Rabbi Akiva, then, as explained, it would involve the equivalent of a denial concerning a deposit and would generate a Torah oath. In that event the Mishnah could not serve to reject Sumchus. The alternative explanation based on an admission to a fine is unavailable to Rav Pappa because he holds that half damages are compensatory rather than a fine.
