Therefore the Gemara establishes the case as one where the injured party says he is uncertain, etc. Rashi's question, however, addresses the final halachic conclusion, according to which half damages are a fine. At that stage the Mishnah can indeed follow Rabbi Akiva. Rashi can therefore ask why the anonymous Gemara challenged only from the last clause rather than from the middle clause as well, and why it did not explain the middle clause by saying that the injured party is fit to take in the presence of witnesses, thereby rejecting the earlier interpretation that the injured party is uncertain. Rashi answers that according to the final ruling, Sumchus does not apply where both parties make definite claims, so it is preferable to preserve the Gemara's establishment of the middle clause in the case of an uncertain injured party, thereby making the clauses parallel. Examine this carefully, and see also what I wrote elsewhere on the subject. None of this, however, is sufficient to sustain the Ramah's explanation. According to him, "fit to take" means simply that the claimant recovers if the tortfeasor stands by his admission, as explained above. The difficulty therefore remains, especially since Tosafot themselves struggled to explain "fit to take but has nothing" as referring to seizure rather than interpreting it like the Ramah. This indicates that Tosafot did not accept the Ramah's approach, contrary to the Shach's assertion that Tosafot also agree with it. There is no need to rely on this inference alone. The view of Tosafot is plainly contrary to the Ramah, as any reader of their words can see. Tosafot explicitly write that the defendant's admission is treated as an admission followed by the claimant's waiver. According to the Ramah, what waiver is there? Moreover, how could it be that even Rabbah bar Natan would agree with Rabban Gamliel that there is an oath of partial admission here if the defendant may say that he was merely mocking the claimant? What partial admission remains upon which to impose an oath? The matter is likewise explicit in Rambam in Hilchot To'en VeNitan. Rambam writes that this case is comparable to one person saying, "I owe you a maneh," and the other responding, "You owe me nothing," in which case the debtor is exempt. In that case the debtor is always exempt even if he continues to stand by his admission. Maharam and the Rosh derive this rule in chapter Yesh Nochalin from the statement, "You admit that you are not our brother." Accordingly, all the Shach's effort to reconcile Rambam with the Ramah was unnecessary, because Rambam's own comparison proves that the exemption remains even where the defendant continues to stand by his admission. Rambam's commentators likewise write this explicitly. What need is there for further length once Rambam, Tosafot, the Baal HaTerumot, the Rosh, the Tur, the Mechaber, Maharshal, and Rama all point in one direction, and, according to what I have written, the Gemara itself strongly supports their view? We therefore rule in accordance with them. The Ramban's view is also clearly the same. The Rosh cites Ramban in Bava Metzia, in the sugya concerning the borrowed and rented animals, as holding that the borrower need not swear that the rented animal died in the ordinary manner. Since the owner claimed concerning the borrowed animal, it is a case of claiming wheat and admitting barley, and he is exempt regarding the barley. See there. In that case the defendant necessarily continues to stand by his statement that the rented animal died normally. Thus Ramban too holds that the exemption applies even where the defendant does not retract. Therefore the primary law is exactly as stated in the Shulchan Aruch, without qualification.

segments.he: דהוי כאלו מחל לו כו' דע כי הרא"ש ס"פ המניח כתב כי רש"י וכן התו' פירשו דלכך פטור משעורים דהוי כאלו מחל לו השעורים וכתב ותמהתי על סברא זו דמילתא דשכיחי שיש לאדם כמה תביעות על חבירו ואין רוצה לתובעם בב"א רק תובע א' מהן ומ"מ לא מחל השאר ועוד דלא דמי הך למתני' דכאן במשנה הוי הודאה שהודה שגדול ולא קטן הזיק ולא מחילה וא"כ אפי' נימא דבמשנה חייב דלא הוי הודאה דנתכוון להרוויח וליטול גדול מ"מ בטענו חיטין פטור משעורים דהוי מחילה וכן אפי' נימא במשנה פטור דה"ל הודאה מ"מ אפשר חייב בשעורים דל"א דמחל: ולכך נ"ל דהך דטענו חיטין ה"ל כעין מתני' דטענו חיטין הלויתיך באותו יום ובאותו שעה והלה אומר שעורים היה אי איתא דהלוהו שניהם היה תובע שניהם כיון דבבת אחת היה אלא מדלא טענו הודה דלא חייב לו שעורים וכו' עכ"ל. והנה רבו בכוונת הרא"ש פירושים מה איכא בין הודאה למחילה. והנה רבינו ירוחם תלמידו כתב בנ"ג ח"ב דלהרא"ש אם עומד הנתבע בדבריו ומחזיקן ואומר שעורים יש לך בידי חייב בשעורים. והנה דבריו צ"ע כי מ"ש הש"ך לפרש דבריו דב"ד אין כופין אותו לשלם שהרי אומר כבר הודה לי אבל הוא מיקרי כגזלן אם לא ישלם. דבריו בלתי מובני' בממ"נ אם אנו אומרים דלא הוי הודא' מחילה למה לא יכופו ב"ד לשלם הרי הודה דחייב שעורים ואיך ינצל דהוא הודה דאין חייב הלא אתה ידעת דשקר אומר ובשטות ידבר ואתה יודע ואומר בב"ד כדברך אז כן עתה דחיי' אתה שעורים ואם הוא חשב ליטול תמורת שעורים חיטין מ"מ אתה יודע דחייב לו שעורים ובמה תפטור אם לא דיטעון הואיל והודה מחל לי והוא הדבר הנרצה דאף בהודאה בריר מחילה א"כ לפ"ז אף מגזל הנתבע פטור דאין לאחר מחילה כלום ולא ידעתי הבדל בין ב"ד לבינו בין עצמו. והמעיין ברי"ו יראה דמתחילה כתב דעת הרמ"ה דיכול לטעון להשטות היה דבריו וכתב לפ"ז בעומד בדבריו חייב בשעורים ואח"כ כתב דעת הרא"ש מטעם הודא' וכתב ולדבריו כמו כן אם עומד בדבריו חייב לשלם הרי דכתב כמו כן דמשמע דשוה בזה לרמ"ה והא התם כופין בב"ד כמ"ש הש"ך. איברא דדעת רי"ו צריך לימוד דלפ"ז ה"ה בעדים מעידים דמ"ש דמודה בע"ד בעצמו ועומד בדבריו או דעדים מעידים דחייב שעורים וא"כ מה דהקשה הרא"ש לרמ"ה דהא משנה דהמניח ע"כ מיירי דעדים ראו נגיחה דאל"כ ה"ל מודה בקנס ופטור תקשה להרא"ש לנפשיה דא"כ דה"ל עדים הא חייב ועוד ודאי דכל המשנה איירי בעומד בדבריו דנגח קטן וליתא בחזרה דבסלע לקה היינו רישא וכמש"ל ובפרט דאיכא עדים ואיך יחזור וא"כ הא לא קשיא כלל מהך דטענו בחיטין. ולמה לנו לשנויא בשנויא דחיקי במשנה ולא אמרי' כפשוטא דמשנה איירי דהמזיק עומד בדבריו וצ"ע דברי ר"י להולמן לכאורה: ומה שנ' בדבריו דזהו ההבדל לדעת הרא"ש ודעת הרמ"ה כפי הבנת רי"ו דהודאה לא ס"ל לרא"ש דהוי מחילה רק הואיל הודאת בע"ד כמאה עדים דמי הרי הוא פוסל כל עדים שיעידו הפכו וכמו שאמרו בגיטין נאמנת עלי ופוסל כל עדים ואף בזו באמרו שאין חייב לו שעורים הרי פוסל כל עדים שיעידו שחייב כי הודאתו יותר מק' עדים אבל מ"מ אם הנתבע מודה שחייב פשיטא דמוציאין דהא כאן הוי איפכא הודאת בע"ד שהוא פוסל לכל עדים שמעידים על הפטור ודבריו נשמעין דמה בכך דהוא מודה דלא היה חייב מ"מ זה שאומר שהוא חייב הרי יכול להתחייב עצמו אפי' במה שאינו חייב כדלעיל סי' מ' וא"כ ודאי דדברי זה קיימים דהתובע נתכוון להרוויח כמ"ש הרא"ש וגם אנו מקיימים דברי שניהם דאמת דלא היה חייב שעורים כלל רק בהודאת פיו מתחייב אעפ"י שאינו חייב וכאודיתא דאיסור גיורא שהיה יודע שאין לרב מרי חלק בפקדון שביד רבא כלל ואף זהו כמוה. והן דברי הרא"ש דלא מחל רק אנן אמרינן דאמת אתו שלא היה חייב שעורים מעולם ולכך לא תבעו שעורים וא"כ עדים אינם מועילים אבל אם הנתבע עומד בדבורו פשיטא דחייב אף דאנן ידעי' דלא הלוהו מעולם שעורים. ולפ"ז לק"מ הא דמדמי הך דשנים רודפים להך דטענו בחיטין אף דבמשנה יש עדים דמה בכך דה"ל עדים לגבי עדים הוי הודאתו יותר וכאלו פסלם כהנ"ל: אך הקו' שני' דמשנה מיירי דמזיק עומד בדבריו י"ל לא מבעיא לפי הנראה מדברי הרא"ש דכתב הסוגיא לפי דקי"ל פ"נ קנסא א"כ קו' הגמרא שפיר דבממ"נ מאיזה טעם יתחייב המזיק לשלם הקטן אם עפ"י עדים הא בהודאתו של הניזק נפסלו עדים וה"ל עדים כמאן דליתא וא"כ לא נשאר רק הודא' פי של המזיק ה"ל מודה בקנס ופטור דכיון דתו ליכא עדים ואלו היה המזיק מכחיש ואמר בסלע לקה פטור ולא היה מועיל העדת עדים כלל.
segments.en: For it is as though he waived it, etc. Know that the Rosh, at the end of chapter HaManiach, writes that Rashi and Tosafot explain that the reason the claimant is exempt from the barley is that he is treated as though he waived the barley. The Rosh writes: I am astonished at this reasoning, because it is common for a person to have several claims against another and not wish to demand all of them at once. He may demand only one of them and nevertheless has not waived the others. Furthermore, this is not comparable to our Mishnah. In the Mishnah there is an admission, for by claiming that the larger ox caused the damage he admitted that the smaller ox did not cause it. This is not a waiver. Therefore, even if we say that in the Mishnah the defendant is liable because the claimant's statement is not treated as an admission, since he intended only to enhance his recovery by claiming the larger ox, it can still be that one who claims wheat is exempt from the barley because his failure to claim the barley constitutes waiver. Conversely, even if we say that in the Mishnah the defendant is exempt because the claimant's statement is an admission, it can still be that in the case of wheat and barley the defendant remains liable for the barley because we do not say that the claimant waived it. I therefore explain the case of claiming wheat as comparable to the Mishnah only where the claimant says, "I lent you wheat on that day and at that hour," and the other responds, "It was barley." If he had lent him both commodities at that same time, he would have claimed both, since they arose simultaneously. His failure to claim the barley therefore constitutes an admission that the defendant does not owe him barley. These are the Rosh's words. Many explanations have been offered regarding the Rosh's intent and the difference between admission and waiver. Rabbenu Yerucham, his student, writes in Netiv 3, part 2, that according to the Rosh, if the defendant stands by his words and affirms them, saying, "You have barley in my possession," he is liable for the barley. His words require study. The Shach explains Rabbenu Yerucham to mean that beit din does not compel the defendant to pay, because the defendant can say that the claimant already admitted that he owes him nothing, but if the defendant himself fails to pay he is considered a robber. This is incomprehensible. Whichever way one looks at it, if we say that the claimant's statement is not an admission that effects waiver, why should beit din not compel payment? The defendant has admitted owing barley. How can he escape by saying, "The claimant admitted that I owe him nothing," when we know that his present contention is false and foolish? We know that he now states in beit din, just as he stated before, that he owes barley. Even if the claimant intended to obtain wheat instead of barley, the defendant himself knows that he owes the barley. On what basis could he be exempt unless he asserts that the claimant's admission operated as a waiver? But that is exactly the point under discussion. If an admission is in fact equivalent to waiver, then the defendant is not even a robber for retaining the money, because nothing remains after a valid waiver. I therefore do not understand the distinction between what beit din may compel and the defendant's obligation toward Heaven. One who examines Rabbenu Yerucham will see that he first cites the view of the Ramah, that the defendant can say his words were uttered merely to mock the claimant. He writes that according to this approach, if the defendant stands by his admission he is liable for the barley. He then cites the Rosh's explanation based on the claimant's admission and writes that according to him likewise, if the defendant stands by his words he must pay. The phrase "likewise" indicates that Rabbenu Yerucham understands the Rosh's rule to be the same as the Ramah's in this respect. According to the Ramah, however, beit din certainly compels payment, as the Shach himself writes. In truth, Rabbenu Yerucham's view requires careful study. According to it, the same should apply where witnesses testify. What difference is there between the defendant himself admitting and standing by his admission that he owes barley and witnesses testifying that he owes barley? If so, the Rosh's question against the Ramah returns against the Rosh himself. The Mishnah in HaManiach necessarily concerns a case where witnesses saw the goring, for otherwise the tortfeasor would be one who admits liability for a fine and would be exempt. If witnesses exist, then according to Rabbenu Yerucham the defendant should be liable. Moreover, the Mishnah certainly concerns a tortfeasor who stands by his statement that the smaller ox gored. There is no question there of retracting and claiming that the injured ox was struck by a rock, for that is the first clause, as I wrote above. This is especially so where witnesses exist, because then he cannot retract at all. If so, the comparison to claiming wheat is no difficulty. Why would we need the strained interpretations that the Gemara gives rather than explaining the Mishnah simply as a case where the tortfeasor continues to stand by his statement? Rabbenu Yerucham's words therefore appear very difficult at first glance. What appears correct in explaining him is that this is precisely the distinction between the Rosh and the Ramah according to Rabbenu Yerucham's understanding. The Rosh does not hold that the claimant's admission itself constitutes waiver. Rather, since an admission by a litigant is equivalent to one hundred witnesses, his admission disqualifies any witnesses who would testify contrary to it, just as the Gemara in Gittin says, "She is believed by me," by which one accepts her statement and effectively rejects contrary witnesses. So too, when the claimant says that the defendant does not owe him barley, he rejects any witnesses who would say that barley is owed, because his own admission is stronger than one hundred witnesses. Nevertheless, if the defendant himself admits that he owes barley, payment is certainly extracted from him. Here the situation is reversed: the defendant's own admission rejects any witnesses that would support his exemption. His own words are accepted. What difference does it make that the claimant previously admitted that no barley was owed? The defendant can impose an obligation upon himself even where no preexisting obligation exists, as stated above in siman 40. Thus his present admission is certainly effective. The claimant may have intended to enhance his claim, as the Rosh writes, and we can preserve both parties' statements. We may say that in truth the defendant never owed barley originally, just as the claimant admitted, but that the defendant now obligates himself through his own admission even though he was not previously liable. This resembles the legal admission made by Issur the convert, who knew that Rav Mari had no actual share in the deposit held by Rava, yet was still able to confer the money through an admission. The same applies here. This is the Rosh's intent. The claimant did not waive anything. Rather, we accept his statement as true that no barley was ever owed, and therefore his claim excluded barley and contrary witnesses are ineffective. But if the defendant stands by his own admission, he is certainly liable, even though we know that no barley was ever lent. According to this, there is no difficulty in comparing the case of two pursuing oxen to the case of wheat and barley even though the Mishnah has witnesses. The existence of witnesses changes nothing, because the claimant's own admission is stronger than the witnesses and is treated as having rejected them, as explained. The second difficulty, that the Mishnah concerns a tortfeasor who stands by his words, can also be resolved. This is obvious according to the Rosh's presentation of the sugya as following the rule that half damages are a fine. The Gemara's question is then straightforward. Whichever basis one might use to obligate the tortfeasor to pay for the smaller ox fails. If the obligation is based upon the witnesses, the injured party's own admission has rejected their testimony. The witnesses are therefore treated as nonexistent. The only remaining basis is the tortfeasor's own admission. But that is an admission to a fine, and one who admits liability for a fine is exempt. Once the witnesses have been neutralized by the claimant's own admission, if the tortfeasor were to deny everything and say that the injured animal was struck by a rock, he would be exempt and the witnesses could no longer help the claimant.

segments.he: אלא אפי' לפי דאמרי' בגמ' דר"פ פריך לימא תהוי תיובתא דרבה ב"נ ור"פ ס"ל פ"נ ממון. יש ליישב ג"כ דבלא"ה צריכין להבין במה דמוקמינן שם דמציעתא מיירי בניזק אומר שמא ומזיק ברי והקשו התו' הא דלא קשיא נמי אמר סומכס בהא דאיצטרך לאשמועי' דלא ותי' הואיל ומודה במקצת ס"ל לסומכס חולקים וכן כתבו התו' אח"כ בד"ה ראוי ליטול בצריכא דרישא קמ"ל אפי' ניזק ברי ומזיק שמא ס"ל לרבנן המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה ובקטן וגדול קמ"ל דאי ניזק שמא ומזיק ברי ס"ל לסומכס יחלוקו ולכאורה ק' הך דתנן ב"מ דף צ"ז השוכר אומר שכורה מתה והלה אומר א"י פטור ומוקמי' ליה בגמ' דמשנה איירי לר"ן במ"מ דתבעהו ג' פרות ובחדא מודה לי' ולכך ברישא ה"ל משאיל"מ וא"כ לסומכס מה בכך דטוען המשאיל שמא כיון דמ"מ הל"ל לסומכס יחלוקו ולא לפטור לגמרי ומשנה דהתם מוקמי' בגמרא כסומכס. וכן בדף ק' במשנה דמחליף בהיה לו שני עבדים המוכר אומר קטן מכרתי והל' אומר א"י זכה בקטן והא שם איירי במ"מ כדאוקמי' שם בהא דתנן ישבע ואיירי בדמי עבד קטן וכו' וא"כ הל"ל יחלוקו לסומכס ומשנה דהתם סומכס היא: ודוחק לומר דבלא"ה הקשו תוס' שם בד"ה מדסיפא וכו' דהא ברי ושמא ברי עדיף וקושי' זו לכ"ע איתא אפי' לר"ן דלא ס"ל ברי עדיף וס"ל הממע"ה דה"מ כשבאין להוציא מיד המוחזק בזו אמרי' אלים חזקת ממון אבל להחזיק ביד המוחזק אף ר"נ מודה דברי עדיף כיון דחזקת המחזיק מסייע. וא"כ בניזק שמא ומזיק ברי הא המזיק מוחזק ולכ"ע ברי עדיף (ובזה מיושב קושי' מהרש"א דהק' דה"ל להקשות ברישא דאיירי בניזק ברי ומזיק שמא דשם אין הקושי' רק לרב יהודה אבל לא לר"נ ולכך הקשה מסיפא דהקושיא היא לכ"ע הואיל והמוחזק טוען ברי ופשוט) וצריך לומר תירוץ התוס' דלא ה"ל למידע וזהו שייך במשנה דהמניח אבל שם בשאלה ושכורה ומשנה דהמחליף לכך בטוען התובע א"י פטור. דברי ושמא ברי עדיף לכ"ע ולא אמר בהו סומכס. כי לפי הנראה מלשון התו' בד"ה מדסיפא דלהך תי' דבמ"מ מודה סומכס אין צורך לתי' השני דה"ל למידע דאל"כ מה וא"ת שכתבו הא דברי עדיף וכו' הא בלא"ה צ"ל כן דאל"כ סותרי' משניות הנ"ל ולא ה"ל למיכתב בלשון קושי' ופירוקא רק תיכף כשכתבו דמודה סומכס במ"מ ה"ל לומר והני מילי במקום דלא ה"ל למיד': וביחוד ק' לשיטת הפוסקים כמש"ל בסי' ע"ה דאפי' דלא ה"ל למידע ברי עדיף. וביותר קשה דא"כ ר"פ דביקש להוכיא דלא מיירי משנה ברי וברי דלא אמר סומכס ברי וברי ומ"מ מוקי למציעת' בניזק אומר שמא ומ"מ ס"ל לסומכס יחלוקו הואיל ומ"מ וכן צ"ל לפי דברי צריכ' דעשו התו' בד"ה ראוי וכו' דאתי' לכ"ע דלמ"ד לא אמר סומכס ברי וברי הך צריכה איך קאי ועכצ"ל דלכ"ע קאי דבמ"מ אפי' בניזק אומר שמא ומזיק ברי ס"ל יחלוקו ולפ"ז כ"ש בניזק אומר ג"כ ברי דודאי עדיף ברי דניזק מאומר שמא וצ"ל במ"מ לכ"ע ס"ל לסומכס יחלוקו אפי' ברי וברי וא"כ קשיא הא דב"מ דף ק' פרכינן תנן זה אומר גדול וזה אומר קטן ישבע בשלמא לא אמר סומכס ברי וברי מש"ה ישבע אלא אמר סומכוס אפי' ברי וברי אמאי ישבע יחלוקו מבעי'. וקשה הא במ"מ כהך משנה דקתני ישבע והיינו מ"מ לכ"ע אמר סומכוס ברי וברי והקו' לכ"ע דהא לא ידע התי' מודה סומכס ביש עסק שבועה. ודוחק לומר דודאי סליק אדעתי' דמקשן תי' הגמרא מודה סומכס בש"ד רק ס"ל למקשן אם התובע עומד וצווח מה לי לשבועתך תן לי החצי כחלוקת סומכס יש לשמוע בקולו דהא יטעון אלו היה כופר בכל היה מגיע לי החצי ובשביל שמוד' מקצת יגרע כחי ואפסיד הכל כי איני מאמינו על השבועה וגם אערומי קמערים הוא להודות בפרוט' כדי לפטור מחלוקה ושפיר ס"ל למקשן דהל"ל יחלוקו והתרצן השיב עכ"פ במקום שבועה לא אמר סומכס דאלו הי' התובע אומר איני רוצה שיהיה חלוקה רק ישבע לי היה צריך הנתבע לעשותו וא"כ אף להיפך כשרוצה התוב' חלוקה יכול הנתבע לומר אני אשבע ואת הטוב נקבל וכו' וזהו למ"ד אמר סומכס ברי וברי אפי' בכופר הכל אבל אי לא אמר סומכס רק במ"מ לא קשה דשפיר ידע מודה סומכס בש"ד ול"ק מגרע גרע ואערומי קמערי' דהא אלו יכפור הכל לא יתחייב בכלום דבברי וברי וכופר הכל מודה סומכס דהממע"ה וכל זה דוחק: ולכן נראה דידוע דמגו דהעזה בשבועה ל"א אבל בממון אמרינן וכמש"ל בכללי מגו באריכות וזהו כמעט מוסכם מכל מחברי': ולפ"ז יש לדייק לפמ"ש דבניזק אומר שמא ומזיק אומר ברי בכופר הכל לא ס"ל לסומכס יחלוקו רק במ"מ וקשה הא יש למזיק מגו דכופר הכל והרי הוא משיב אבידה ואי דאמרי' כדרבה מפני מה אמרה תורה מ"מ וכו' משום דחזקה אין אדם מעיז וה"ל מגו דהעז'. תינח אם באנו לדון לפוטרו משבועה הא אנן ממון פטרינן וצ"ל דכאן מיירי דיש עדים על נגיחה רק לא ידעו מי נגח קטן או גדול וא"כ תו ליכא מגו דא"י להכחיש העדים אבל במקום דליכא עדים לכ"ע אף במ"מ ס"ל לסומכ' דלא יחלוקו דהא יש למזיק מגו דכופר הכל ובממון לא משגיחין בהעזה כלל. ולפ"ז כל הנ"ל מיושב דשם כל הנך משניות לא איירי בעדים וא"כ מודה סומכס הממע"ה ולכך קתני פטור וקושי' הגמרא שפיר דלמ"ד לא אמר סומכס ברי וברי בכופר הכל לא קשה יחלוקו דמה בכך דה"ל מ"מ מ"מ הא יש לו מגו דכופר הכל ולא אמר סומכס ברי וברי ודוק: ואף דלר"פ דס"ל פ"נ ממון ואצ"ל דמשנה דוקא בעדי' איירי מ"מ משנה סתמא קתני הן ישנו עדים והן ליכא עדים ואיצטריך לאשמועי' דלא כסומכס דס"ל בישנו עדים יחלוקו וקמ"ל דלא דמ"מ הממע"ה כחכמים וא"ש ולפ"ז גם סוגי' דגמ' אליבא דר"פ לשיטת רי"ו יש ליישב דכך המשך דברי הגמרא (ולא קשה דילמא מיירי דמזי' עומד בדבורים) מדרישא ברי וברי סיפא נמי ברי וברי וק' תרתי ל"ל אלא צ"ל רישא קמ"ל כחו דסומכס דאמר אפי' ברי וברי יחלוקו וסיפא דחכמים פליגי עליה אפי' במ"מ וקשה פשיטא דהא ה"ל מגו דכופר הכל וא"כ אי פליגי ברישא ע"כ בסיפא נמי פליגי וכמו כן אי ס"ל לסומכס במ"מ יחלוקו אף בכופר הכל נמי ס"ל כן דאל"כ ה"ל מגו כהנ"ל ותרתי ל"ל ואי דיש כאן עדים וא"א לכפור הכל נימא תהוי תיובתא דרבה ב"נ בטענו בחיטין דה"ל הודאה ופוסל לעדים וא"כ אם ירצה המזיק יכול לכפור דעדים נפסלים בהודאתו וא"כ חזר הדבר דה"ל מגו וקשה תרתי ל"ל ואי איירי מצעיתא בניזק אומר ברי ומזיק שמא קשה הא לא כי קתני וצ"ל כמ"ש התו' דבברי וברי נמי איירי ורישא דקתני לא כי אף דמיירי דומי' דסיפא ברי ושמא מ"מ בברי וברי נמי איירי וק' הא לא איירי סומכס ביה ולמה נשנה במשנה בשלמא אי חד דוקא תני אידך איידי אף דלא איירי סומכס בהו וכמ"ש מהרש"א משא"כ אי בכל גוונא לא איירי סומכס א"כ לא כי מיותר ועכצ"ל דבסיפא דאיכא מ"מ איירי סומכס אפי' בברי וברי ואיצטרך לא כי ותנא רישא איידי דסיפא ופריך הגמ' אכתי תיובתא דרב"נ דהא יש לו מגו דכופר הכל ואי עדים הא פסלו לעדים ולכך מוקי ליה בניזק אומר שמא ומזיק ברי ומדויק לא כי ותנא רישא איידי דסיפא אף דלא איירי ביה סומכס ולק"מ ודוק כי חריף הוא. וזהו שכתבתי לפי גי' שגרסו ר"פ אבל מדברי הרא"ש נראה דלא גריס ר"פ וס"ל דכל הסוגיא למ"ד פ"נ קנסא וא"כ בלא"ה א"ש ועכ"פ זהו ברבינו ירוחם ברור ונכון. ובאמת יש סמך לדברי רי"ו דהודאה לא ס"ל להרא"ש מחילה מהא דכתב הרא"ש בפ"ב דכתובות האומר שטר אמנה הוא זה במקום שחב לאחרים אינו נאמן והקשה הרא"ש הא ה"ל מגו דמחיל' ותי' הרא"ש דאינו רוצה להפסיד חובו ואם מחיל לא ישלם הלוה אבל באומר אמנה יודע שאין הלוה גזלן וק' הא אף עכשיו דאומר אמנה והודה שלא הלוהו מעולם ה"ל מחילה וא"כ עדיין אין הלוה גזלן והיינו הך דמודה דלא הלוהו שעורים דמ"ש דלא הלוהו שעורים או דלא הלוה זה השטר ולא ידעתי הבדל. ודוחק לומר דשם הוי הודאה רק להבריח מב"ח ולא הודאה שלימה דא"כ אף במחילה כן דאין זה מחילה בלב ודוחק לחלק: אך עם כל זה מסתימת דברי הטור משמע דלא ס"ל כרי"ו דא"כ ה"ל לומר דבעומד בדבריו דחייב ואיך השמיט הך דינא ובפרט כפי מ"ש לחלק בין דישנו עדים ובין דעומד בדבריו: וכן ברא"ש ק' דאם יש הבדל בין הודאה למחילה למה נאיד מפירש"י ותו' דהטעם משום מחילה ואי דהקש' דמעשה בכל יום שאדם יש לו כמה תביעות ואין תובע רק אחד נישני כמו דשני לנפשיה דמיירי דשני תביעות הן בזמן ושעה אחת וא"כ מדלא תבע שניהם ש"מ דמחיל להשני וכמו דאומר הרא"ש בהודאה. אלא ברור דהיא היא מחילה היא היא הודאה דהודה הוי מטעם מחילה דלכך הודאת בע"ד כק' עדים משום דמחיל כדאמרינן לעיל סע"ה כמש"ל באודייתא דאוסר גיורא ואדרבא נראה דאי הטעם משום מחילה לא יתכן בפקדון כמ"ש אבל אי הטעם משום הודאה אף בפקדון יתכן כמו אודייתא דאיסר הנ"ל רק ודאי אף רש"י ס"ל דמדלא תבע הודה כמ"ש הרא"ש דגבי מתני' דהמניח לא שייך מחילה רק הודאה רק רש"י ס"ל הואיל וסתם אמרו טענו חיטין והודה בשעורים אף דלא היה בזמן א' משמע כמ"ש מהרש"ל ובזה לא שייך מדלא תבע הודה לגבי' דאין אדם תובע כא' כל תביעות ולכך ס"ל לרש"י משום מחיל' א"כ י"ל כמ"ש מהרש"ל הואיל והוא הודה בשעורים והוא לא השיב תיכף תוך כ"ד אף שעורים יש לי בידך ש"מ מחיל וע"ז הקשה הרא"ש דאין כאן ראיה דאין אדם תובע כל תביעות וא"כ מה היה צורך לו לומר אף שעורים כיון דאינו תובעו כעת וע"כ צ"ל דהיה השל בזמן ושעה אחת א"כ השתא דאתינא לדין אין תו כלל צורך לומר מחילה רק הודאה כמ"ש גבי שור שרדף אחר שור אבל באמת אותו זמן ושעה אין הבדל בין הודאה למחילה: ואדרבא עדיף כמ"ש. ויש עוד ראיה דבב"מ בשמעת' דשאלה ושכורה חישב הרמב"ן לדמותו לטוענו בחיטין והודה בשעורים כתב הרא"ש דלא מחוור דבשלמא בטענו בחיטין וכו' מחל לו השעורים כמ"ש רש"י בפ' המניח וכו': וכן סיים לבסוף מדלא טענו מחל לו עליהם או הודה שאין לו שעורים ומדתפס פירש"י אלו לא ס"ל לא היה לו להביא פירש"י מה דלא ס"ל רק פירושו וכן מה שסיים מחל או הודה ש"מ דלדינא אם הוא בזמן ושעה אחת לאו נ"מ ודא ודא אחת היא וזה ברור ובפרט לפי מ"ש רי"ו דאם עומד בדיבורו לא שייך טענו בחיטין הלא שם השוכר עומד בדיבורו דשכורה מתה ואיך יפטור בטוענו שאולה כמ"ש הרמב"ן שם אלא וודאי דזה אינו ודברי הרא"ש אלו היה בהעלם עין בהמחברים שלא הביאו כלל ראיה מהך דהרא"ש מפרש להדיא דאף הודאה הוי מחילה:
segments.en: But even according to the version of the Gemara in which Rav Pappa asks whether the Mishnah refutes Rabbah bar Natan, and Rav Pappa holds that half damages are compensatory, the matter can still be explained. Quite apart from our issue, one must understand the Gemara's establishment of the middle clause as a case where the injured party says he is uncertain and the tortfeasor makes a definite claim. Tosafot ask why this clause is not also needed to reject Sumchus. They answer that since there is partial admission, Sumchus would say that the parties divide. Tosafot later write, s.v. ra'ui litol, that the clauses are both necessary. The first clause teaches that even where the injured party makes a definite claim and the tortfeasor is uncertain, the Sages still apply the rule that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant. The case of the larger and smaller ox teaches that where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor is certain, Sumchus nevertheless requires division. At first glance this is difficult from the Mishnah in Bava Metzia 97, where the renter says that the rented animal died and the owner says that he does not know, and the renter is exempt. The Gemara establishes that Mishnah, according to Rav Nachman, as a case of partial admission: the owner claimed three cows and the renter admitted one. Accordingly, in the first clause he is one who cannot swear and must pay. If so, according to Sumchus, why should it matter that the owner says he is uncertain? Since there is partial admission, Sumchus should require division rather than a complete exemption. Yet the Gemara there establishes the Mishnah according to Sumchus. Similarly, in Bava Metzia 100, where the Mishnah discusses one who exchanged property and where there were two slaves, the seller says, "I sold the smaller one," and the buyer says, "I do not know," the smaller slave is awarded to the buyer. That case too involves partial admission, as the Gemara establishes in explaining the clause requiring an oath, namely that the dispute concerns the value of the smaller slave, etc. If so, Sumchus should require division there as well, yet that Mishnah too is according to Sumchus. It is strained to answer merely that Tosafot there already ask, s.v. midsifa, that in a definite claim against an uncertain claim the definite claim should prevail. This question exists even according to Rav Nachman, who does not generally hold that a definite claim prevails. Rav Nachman rejects that principle only where the definite claimant seeks to extract money from the possessor, because the possessor's monetary chazakah is powerful. But where the possessor himself makes the definite claim, even Rav Nachman agrees that the definite claim is superior, since the possessor's chazakah supports it. Accordingly, where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor is certain, the tortfeasor is in possession and everyone should agree that his definite claim prevails. This also resolves the Maharsha's question why Tosafot did not ask from the first clause, where the injured party is certain and the tortfeasor uncertain. There the question exists only according to Rav Yehudah, not according to Rav Nachman. Tosafot therefore ask from the latter clause, where the possessor himself makes the definite claim, so the question applies according to all opinions. The answer must then be Tosafot's second resolution, that this is a matter the injured party could not have known. That answer works in the Mishnah in HaManiach, but in the Mishnah concerning the borrowed and rented animals and in the Mishnah concerning the exchange, where the claimant says he does not know, the defendant is exempt because the definite claim is stronger for all opinions and Sumchus does not require division. Yet from Tosafot's wording in s.v. midsifa it appears that once we use the answer that Sumchus agrees in a case of partial admission, there is no need for the second answer that the claimant could not have known. Otherwise, why would Tosafot formulate the latter point as a separate question and answer, "But is not a definite claim superior?" If that distinction were independently necessary to reconcile the other Mishnayot, Tosafot should have stated immediately, after saying that Sumchus agrees in partial admission, that this is true only where the claimant could not have known. This is especially difficult according to the authorities, as discussed above in siman 75, who hold that even where the claimant could not have known, a definite claim is superior. There is an even greater difficulty. Rav Pappa sought to prove that the Mishnah does not deal with two definite claims because Sumchus does not apply where both parties are certain. Nevertheless, he establishes the middle clause as a case where the injured party is uncertain, and Tosafot's explanation requires that, because there is partial admission, Sumchus would require division. Likewise, Tosafot's necessity analysis in s.v. ra'ui, which applies according to all opinions, must mean that even according to the view that Sumchus does not apply where both parties are certain, the rule of division applies in a case of partial admission where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor is certain. If that is so, all the more so where the injured party also makes a definite claim. A definite claim by the injured party is stronger than an uncertain claim. It would therefore follow that where there is partial admission, everyone agrees that Sumchus requires division even when both parties are certain. But this is difficult from Bava Metzia 100. The Gemara there asks from the Mishnah: one says that he sold the larger slave and the other says the smaller, and the defendant must swear. This is understandable according to the view that Sumchus does not apply where both parties are certain, for then he swears. But according to the view that Sumchus applies even where both are certain, why should he swear? They should divide. Yet that very Mishnah involves partial admission, as indicated by the obligation to swear. According to the reasoning above, Sumchus should require division there according to all opinions, even according to the view that he does not ordinarily apply his rule to two definite claims. The Gemara's question should therefore arise according to everyone, even before it knows the answer that Sumchus agrees where there is a Torah oath. It is difficult to answer that the questioner certainly anticipated the Gemara's eventual answer that Sumchus agrees where a Torah oath exists, but nevertheless reasoned that if the claimant protests, "What do I care about your oath? Give me half under Sumchus's rule," we should listen to him. He could argue that if the defendant had denied everything, the claimant would have received half, so why should the claimant's position be weakened and he lose everything merely because the defendant admitted a small part? Perhaps the defendant is strategically admitting a perutah in order to escape division. The questioner would then be understood as saying that they should divide, while the answer would be that in any event, once the Torah imposes an oath, Sumchus's division rule does not apply. If the claimant had demanded an oath rather than division, the defendant would have had to swear. Conversely, when the claimant seeks division, the defendant may say, "I am prepared to swear, and we shall accept whichever result the Torah gives." This might explain why the question is raised only according to the view that Sumchus applies to two definite claims even in total denial. According to the view that Sumchus does not apply except where there is partial admission, the possibility of strategic partial admission creates no difficulty, for if the defendant denied everything he would owe nothing in a case of two definite claims. Still, this entire explanation is strained. It therefore appears that a recognized rule is decisive here: a migo that would require brazenness is not accepted to exempt one from an oath, but it is accepted with respect to monetary liability, as I discussed at length above in the rules of migo. This is almost unanimously accepted by the authorities. Accordingly, consider the case discussed above where the injured party says he is uncertain and the tortfeasor says he is certain. If the tortfeasor totally denied liability, Sumchus would not require division, but where he partially admits liability Tosafot say that Sumchus does require division. This seems difficult because the tortfeasor has a migo that he could have denied everything. He is therefore like one who returns a lost item voluntarily. One might answer, following Rabbah's explanation of why the Torah imposes an oath on one who partially admits a claim, that a person generally does not have the brazenness to deny the entire claim. But that answer works only if we seek to exempt him from an oath. Here we seek to exempt him from monetary liability, and with respect to money we do accept even a migo that involves brazenness. We must therefore say that the Mishnah concerns a case where witnesses saw the goring but did not know whether the larger or smaller ox caused it. The tortfeasor then has no migo to deny everything, because he cannot contradict the witnesses. Where there are no witnesses, everyone agrees that even in a case of partial admission Sumchus does not require division, because the tortfeasor has a migo that he could have denied everything, and with respect to money we disregard the brazenness involved. Accordingly, all the Mishnayot cited above are resolved. Those Mishnayot do not concern cases supported by witnesses. Sumchus therefore agrees that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant, and this is why they teach complete exemption. The Gemara's question is also precise. According to the view that Sumchus does not apply where both parties make definite claims and the defendant totally denies liability, there is no question that they should divide. Even if the defendant partially admits, he has a migo that he could have denied everything, and since Sumchus does not apply in two definite claims with total denial, that migo defeats division. This applies in the absence of witnesses. Even though Rav Pappa holds that half damages are compensatory, so that it is not necessary to say that the Mishnah specifically deals with witnesses, the Mishnah is stated without qualification and includes both a case where witnesses exist and one where they do not. It is therefore necessary to teach the Sages' position against Sumchus in the case where witnesses do exist. Sumchus would require division there, and the Mishnah teaches that even there the Sages say that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant. This properly explains the matter. According to Rabbenu Yerucham's understanding, the sugya can therefore be read as follows, even according to Rav Pappa. One cannot answer simply that the tortfeasor stands by his statement. Since the first clause involves two definite claims, the latter clause should likewise involve two definite claims. If so, why are both clauses necessary? We might answer that the first teaches the strength of Sumchus's rule, that even with two definite claims they divide, while the second teaches the strength of the Sages, that even with partial admission they disagree and require proof. But that would itself be obvious, because in the absence of witnesses the tortfeasor has a migo to deny everything. If the Sages reject Sumchus in the first clause, then certainly they reject him in the latter clause. Conversely, if Sumchus requires division in a case of partial admission even though the defendant could totally deny, then he must also apply his rule where there is total denial. The two clauses would again be redundant. If we say that witnesses exist, so that the defendant cannot deny everything, then the case should constitute a refutation of Rabbah bar Natan. The claimant's assertion of wheat is an admission that rejects the witnesses concerning barley. If so, once the witnesses are rejected by his admission, the tortfeasor could again deny the barley entirely, and the migo problem returns. Thus both clauses would remain unnecessary. If the middle clause instead concerns a definite claim by the injured party and uncertainty by the tortfeasor, the wording "No, rather" becomes difficult. Tosafot therefore explain that even if the first clause includes a case of definite claims and the latter clause a case of uncertainty, the first may still have been stated alongside the second. But then the comparison to Sumchus does not work unless the latter clause, because of its partial admission, is a case in which Sumchus applies even where both parties make definite claims. That makes the phrase "No, rather" meaningful, and the first clause is then taught incidentally because of the second. The Gemara can consequently challenge Rabbah bar Natan precisely. Since the defendant has a migo to deny everything, and if witnesses exist the claimant's own admission has rejected those witnesses, how can the partial admission generate a different result? The Gemara therefore establishes the case as one where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor is certain. The phrase "No, rather" is then precise, and the first clause is taught incidentally because of the second even though Sumchus does not apply to the first in exactly the same manner. This resolves the matter. Examine it carefully, for the reasoning is subtle. All of this follows the version that reads Rav Pappa in the sugya. From the Rosh's words, however, it appears that he did not have the reading of Rav Pappa and understood the entire discussion as following the opinion that half damages are a fine. According to that version the matter is, in any event, readily explained as stated above. This, at least, provides a clear and correct explanation of Rabbenu Yerucham. There is in fact support for Rabbenu Yerucham's understanding that the Rosh does not identify admission with waiver. In chapter 2 of Ketubot the Rosh discusses one who says, "This promissory note is a note of accommodation." Where this statement causes a loss to others, he is not believed. The Rosh asks why he is not believed through a migo that he could simply waive the debt. He answers that the creditor does not wish to lose the debt. If he waived it, the borrower would no longer have to pay him, whereas by saying that the note is merely a note of accommodation he knows that the borrower is not a robber. This is difficult. Even now, by saying that the note is fictitious and admitting that he never lent the money, his statement should itself amount to a waiver. The borrower would therefore still not be a robber. What difference is there between admitting that no barley was lent and admitting that the loan represented by this promissory note never occurred? I see no distinction. It is strained to say that there his admission was made only to keep the debt away from his own creditors and is therefore not a complete admission. If so, the same should apply to an ostensible waiver, for in his heart he does not intend to waive. It is difficult to distinguish between them. Nevertheless, the plain implication of the Tur is that he does not accept Rabbenu Yerucham's view. If he did, he should have stated that where the defendant stands by his admission, he must pay. How could the Tur omit such a significant law, especially if, as explained above, there is a distinction between a case with witnesses and a case where the defendant himself continues to stand by his admission? There is also a difficulty in the Rosh himself. If there is a genuine distinction between admission and waiver, why did he depart from Rashi and Tosafot, who explain the exemption as resulting from waiver? His objection was that it happens every day that a person has several claims and demands only one of them. But the Rosh could have answered Rashi exactly as he answers for himself, namely that the case is one where the two claims arose at the same time and in the same transaction. In that circumstance, by failing to claim both at once, the claimant has waived the second, just as the Rosh says that his omission constitutes an admission. Why then reject Rashi's explanation at all? Rather, it is clear that the two concepts are really one. The claimant's admission operates because it is treated as waiver. This is why a litigant's admission is equivalent to one hundred witnesses, because through his admission he relinquishes his right, as explained above in siman 75 and in my discussion of the admission of Issur the convert. Indeed, waiver is the stronger and more natural concept here. If the reason were only admission, it could apply even to a deposit, just like Issur's admission, whereas pure waiver is more difficult to apply to property that remains legally in the depositor's possession, as I wrote above. Rashi too certainly agrees that the claimant's failure to demand the barley is treated as an admission, just as the Rosh says regarding the Mishnah in HaManiach, where waiver does not naturally apply and the operative idea is admission. The difference is only that Rashi understood the general statement, "he claimed wheat and admitted barley," to apply even where the two alleged debts did not arise at the same time. As Maharshal writes, in such a case there is no inference from the fact that the claimant did not demand barley, because a person does not necessarily demand all his separate claims at once. Rashi therefore explains the waiver differently. Since the defendant admitted barley and the claimant did not immediately respond, within the time required for speech, "You also owe me barley," his silence demonstrates that he waived the barley. The Rosh objects that there is no such proof. Since a person need not pursue all his claims at once, there was no reason for the claimant to say anything about the barley when he was not presently demanding it. The Rosh therefore concludes that the case must involve claims arising at the same time and in the same transaction. Once we reach that conclusion, there is no need to describe the result as an independent waiver. The claimant's omission itself is an admission, exactly as in the case of one ox pursuing another. But in truth, where both liabilities arose at the same time, there is no practical distinction between admission and waiver. On the contrary, the concepts reinforce each other. There is further proof from Bava Metzia in the sugya of the borrowed and rented animals. Ramban sought to compare that case to one who claims wheat and the defendant admits barley. The Rosh rejects the comparison and writes: in the case of wheat and barley, the claimant waived the barley, as Rashi explains in chapter HaManiach, etc. He concludes there that because the claimant did not claim the barley, he waived it or admitted that no barley was owed. Had the Rosh disagreed with Rashi's concept of waiver, there would have been no reason for him to cite Rashi's explanation. The Rosh's formulation, "he waived it or admitted that it was not owed," likewise shows that, as a matter of law where the claims arise at the same time, there is no difference between the two formulations. They are two descriptions of the same legal effect. This is especially compelling against Rabbenu Yerucham's rule that if the defendant stands by his admission, the rule of wheat and barley no longer applies. In the case of the borrowed and rented animals the renter unquestionably stands by his statement that the rented animal died in the ordinary manner. Yet Ramban applies the wheat and barley principle, and the Rosh discusses the comparison without saying that continued adherence to the admission removes the exemption. It is therefore clear that Rabbenu Yerucham's qualification is not correct. The Rosh's own words, which the later authorities did not cite in this connection, explicitly show that even an admission is treated as waiver for purposes of this law.

segments.he: ובשעה פלונית וכו' זהו דעת הרא"ש והיש"ש כתב דלישנא סתם נאמר משמע אפי' לא היו שתיהן ביום א' ובקושי' הרא"ש כתב כיון לאחר שזה הודה בשעורים וחזר ותבעו חיטין ולא הזכיר בתביעתו שעורים ש"מ מחל לו. וכתב הש"ך דאף הרא"ש מודה לדינא אם הנדון כמ"ש מהרש"ל דחזר לתבעו חיטין אף דלא נעשו שני הלואות כאחד פטור משעורים. רק הרא"ש דחיק' לי' לפרש כן במילתא דרבה ב"נ ובשגם שהוא הקשה עוד קושי' לפירש"י משום מחילה ע"ש. ולענ"ד נראה דמדברי תו' יש הוכחה לדברי מהרש"ל וגם הרא"ש דס"ל משום הודאה כוונתו ג"כ כשחזר לתבוע חיטין אז הוי הודא' ולא מקדם ועם כל זה לא ס"ל מחילה דמה בכך דחזר לתבעו חיטין כיון דלא נעשו כאחד לא השגיח לתבעו דקשי' לי במה דכתבו התו' ד"ה לימא וכו' דהקשו דילמא משנה ר"ג היא דס"ל טענו בחיטין והודה בשעורים חייב ותי' התו' דאף ר"ג מודה דמשעורים פטור לשלם רק מ"מ חייב שבועת מ"מ ע"ש: ואנכי לא הבנתי התובע לחבירו ואמר יש לי בידך ק' זהובים וחמשין מחולים לך וחמשי' פרע לי והנתבע השיב לא חייבתי לך רק חמשים והם מחולי' ממך וכי ס"ד שיהיה חייב שבועת מ"מ הא לא הודה לו בכלום ואין לך כופר בכל יותר מזה. ולכן היה נראה דס"ל לתו' כמהרש"ל דבתביע' ראשונה עדיין אין מחול לו דאין אדם תובע הכל בב"א רק כשהודה שעורים וחזר לתבוע חיטין אז נעשה עיקר המחילה. וא"כ בשעת הודאת הנתבע בשעורים היה הודאה גמורה עדיין דאם לא היה חוזר התובע לדבריו ראשונים היה מחייב שעורים והוי הודאה גמורה לחייב שבועת מ"מ וא"ש וזה ברור. וגם ברא"ש דבהשיגו על הרי"ף דלענין שעורים לא מהני תפיסה כתב דלדמי חיטין א"י לתופסן דהרי כופר בה ולא מהני תפיס' בעדים ונפטר בשבועה לר"ג ולרבנן אפי' בלי שבועה ולשעורים לא מהני תפיסה שהרי כבר הודה או מחל עליהם וכו' עכ"ל. הרי דתפס בפשיטות דמשעורים פטור לכ"ע ולענין שבועה העמידו במחלוקת ר"ג ורבנן וש"מ דמ"מ חייב שבועה לר"ג וקושיא הנ"ל במקומו וצ"ל להרא"ש ג"כ עיקר הודאה הוא במה שאומר אח"כ שני' לתבוע חיטין ואז ה"ל הודאה אבל מתחילה לא הוה הודאה וא"כ כשהודה הנתבע ממון מעליא הודה וה"ל מ"מ לר"ג. וא"כ צ"ל דס"ל לרא"ש כשאין נעשים בזמן אחד מ"מ לא הוי הודאה אפי' חזר לדבריו הראשונים ומ"ש הש"ך ראיה מרי"ו אין ראיה דשם כתב באומר לא כי אלא חיטין ובזה לא יפול ספק באומר לא כי דמוחל על שאר דהרי אומר לא כי אבל בסתם אף שחזר לתביעתו הראשונה מ"מ שפיר י"ל לא רציתי לתבוע הלואה שנעשית בזמן אחר מאיזה טעם:
segments.en: And at a particular time, etc. This is the view of the Rosh. Maharshal, in Yam Shel Shlomo, writes that the formulation is stated without qualification and therefore implies that the rule applies even if the two loans did not occur on the same day. Addressing the Rosh's difficulty, he explains that after the defendant admitted the barley, the claimant returned to demanding wheat and did not mention barley in his renewed claim. This demonstrates that he waived the barley. The Shach writes that even the Rosh agrees with this rule where the circumstances are as Maharshal describes, namely that the claimant returned and again demanded wheat. Even if the two loans did not arise together, he is then exempt from the barley. The Rosh merely found it strained to interpret Rabbah bar Natan's statement in this manner, especially since the Rosh raised another difficulty against Rashi's explanation based on waiver. See there. In my opinion, Tosafot provide proof for Maharshal's view. Moreover, even the Rosh, who explains the rule in terms of admission, means that the admission occurs only when the claimant returns and again demands the wheat, not beforehand. Nevertheless, the Rosh still does not accept that this is a waiver where the two loans did not arise together, because the fact that the claimant returned to demand wheat proves nothing about the separate barley debt. Since the two debts did not arise together, he had no reason to concern himself with demanding the other one at that time. My difficulty is with Tosafot, s.v. leima, who ask why the Mishnah could not follow Rabban Gamliel, who holds that where one claims wheat and the defendant admits barley, the defendant is liable. Tosafot answer that even Rabban Gamliel agrees that the defendant is exempt from paying the barley itself. Rabban Gamliel holds only that the admission nevertheless creates an oath of partial admission. See there. I do not understand this. Suppose a claimant says to another, "You owe me one hundred gold coins. Fifty are waived to you, and pay me the other fifty," and the defendant responds, "I never owed you except fifty, and those fifty are waived by you." Could one imagine that the defendant is liable for an oath of partial admission? He has admitted owing nothing that remains payable. There could be no clearer case of total denial. It therefore appears that Tosafot agree with Maharshal. On the claimant's first demand there is not yet any waiver, because a person does not necessarily demand all his claims at once. Only after the defendant admits barley and the claimant then returns to demand wheat does the principal waiver occur. Accordingly, at the moment when the defendant admitted the barley, his statement was still a complete and effective monetary admission. Had the claimant not returned to his original demand, the defendant would have been liable for the barley. That initial admission is therefore sufficient to create the status of partial admission and the accompanying oath. This is clear. The same must be said in the Rosh. In his criticism of the Rif, who holds that seizure does not help with respect to the barley, the Rosh writes that the claimant cannot retain the value of the wheat, because the defendant denies that obligation and seizure in the presence of witnesses does not help. The defendant is exempt upon taking an oath according to Rabban Gamliel, and according to the Sages even without an oath. As for the barley, seizure does not help because the claimant has already admitted that it was not owed or has waived it. These are his words. The Rosh clearly assumes that everyone agrees that the barley itself is exempt, while he makes the obligation to swear depend upon the dispute between Rabban Gamliel and the Sages. Thus, according to Rabban Gamliel, there remains an oath of partial admission. The difficulty just stated therefore applies equally to the Rosh. We must consequently say that according to the Rosh as well, the decisive admission by the claimant occurs only when he subsequently reiterates his demand for wheat. Before that renewed demand, there was no admission. At the time the defendant first admitted barley, therefore, he made a genuine monetary admission. His statement constituted partial admission for purposes of Rabban Gamliel's oath. It follows, however, that the Rosh must hold that where the two debts did not arise at the same time, the claimant's renewed demand of wheat still does not amount to an admission concerning the barley. The Shach's proof from Rabbenu Yerucham is not compelling, because Rabbenu Yerucham speaks of a claimant who says, "No, rather it was wheat." The expression "No, rather" leaves no room for doubt that he rejects the barley entirely and thereby relinquishes any other claim, for he explicitly says "No." But where the claimant merely repeats his original demand without that formulation, even after the defendant has mentioned barley, one may still say that he simply chose not to demand a separate loan that arose at another time, for whatever reason.

segments.he: ואין לדקדק ברא"ש דבלא"ה קשה שבועה זו מה טיבו הא תפס שעורים וא"כ זהו שמודה בשעורים ה"ל הילך דכבר דמי הודאתו בידו די"ל לפי סברא זו שהרא"ש עסק בה דלכך מהני תפיסה משום בממ"נ או תן לי שעורים או אני תוספו לדמי חיטין אף תפיסה לאחר שעמדו בדין מהני ותו לא הוה ליה הילך דאז בשעת הודאה לא היה הילך ופשוט: ואין לדקדק ה"ל להרא"ש להוכיח בקיצור דאי איירי בטענו חיטין והודה לו בשעורי' לא שהיה הלואת שעורים בב"א רק לאחר זמן ומדלא תבעו מחל לו א"כ מה אתיא טענו חיטין והודה לו בשעורים אפי' תבעו חיטין בניסן והודה לו בחיטין בתשרי יפטור מדלא תבע הלואת תשרי ש"מ מחל לו די"ל דס"ל להרא"ש כמ"ש בשמעת' דשאלה ושכורה דבין חיטין לשעורין לא טעו אינשי וא"כ בזמן י"ל דטעו בין תשרי לניסן וא"כ י"ל היינו הך דתשרי ואם הוא אומר בניסן טעה וא"ש. מיהו לפמ"ש די"ל דמ"מ חייב שבועה אף דפטור משעורים רק רבנן פליגי משום דס"ל דלא הוה ממין טענה א"כ י"ל בחיטין וחיטין הוי ממין טענה ואינו פטור משבועה ורבה ב"נ פטור לגמרי קאמר אך אין זו מספיק דהא בהודה כפי אותן סך חיטין שתבעו מה כפירה יש כאן. ומה מ"מ יש כאן.
segments.en: And one should not infer against the Rosh that, in any event, this oath itself is difficult. The claimant has seized the barley, so the amount admitted is already in his hands and would seem to be heilech, since the very money corresponding to the defendant's admission is already possessed by the claimant. One may answer that according to the reasoning the Rosh was discussing, seizure works because of a whichever way you look at it argument: either give me the barley, or I will retain what I seized toward the value of the wheat. On that theory, even seizure after the parties have already appeared in judgment is effective. It therefore is not heilech, because at the time of the defendant's admission the admitted amount was not yet in the claimant's hands. This is straightforward. Nor should one argue that the Rosh could have proven his position more simply. If claiming wheat and admitting barley referred to a barley loan made at another time, and the claimant's failure to demand that barley loan constituted waiver, then the same should be true even where he claimed wheat lent in Nisan and the defendant admitted wheat lent in Tishrei. The defendant should be exempt because the claimant did not demand the Tishrei loan and therefore evidently waived it. One may answer that the Rosh writes in the sugya of the borrowed and rented animals that people do not confuse wheat with barley. By contrast, they may confuse times. The claimant may confuse Tishrei with Nisan. Accordingly, where both claims concern wheat, the defendant can say that the loan he admits is the very loan being claimed, except that the claimant erred regarding the date. This resolves the point. Still, according to what I wrote, one could say that even when the barley itself is exempt, an oath may remain because the defendant made a partial admission, while the Sages exempt him from the oath only because they hold that the admission must be of the same kind as the claim. If so, where both claims concern wheat, the admission is certainly of the same kind as the claim and the defendant would not be exempt from an oath. Rabbah bar Natan, however, states a complete exemption. Yet this is not a sufficient answer either, because if the defendant admitted the same quantity of wheat that the claimant demanded, there is no denied amount at all. What partial admission would there be upon which to impose an oath?

segments.he: ואם תפס זהו דעת הרי"ף והרמב"ם ואולם הרא"ש הקשה לשיטתו דא"כ אף במציעתא ה"ל לומר בדתפס ולא בדניזק אמר שמא ומזיק אומר ברי: והש"ך כתב ליישבו וטרם שנעיין בישובו צריכין אנו להבין קושי' הרא"ש דהא לימא הרא"ש לנפשיה לימא בתרווייהו בדניזק אומר שמא ומזיק ברי וצ"ל כתי' התו' ורש"י דתרתי ל"ל א"כ אף להרי"ף אי איירי ג"כ בדתפס תרתי ל"ל ואמת כי הרא"ש נזהר מזה וכת' דמציעתא ה"ל לאוקמי בדתפס וסיפא בברי ושמא. אבל לא מובן כל הצורך דמה נרוויח סוף כל סוף יהיה הקושיא על רבה בר ממל דלא איירי ברי וברי דודאי רישא ומציעתא וסיפא דמי' להדדי ובאמת סיפא איירי בניזק אומר ברי ומזיק שמא ובדתפס ומציעת' להיפוך מזיק אומר ברי וניזק שמא ורישא מזיק שמא וניזק ברי ודמיא להדדי כדאמרי' בגמ' דסוף סוף איכא ברי ושמא בכל בבא וא"כ אי נהפך התי' יהיה מ"מ דומי' ויהיה סיפא ניזק שמא ומזיק ברי ומציעתא ורישא יהיה בניזק ברי ומזיק שמא ומציעתא בדתפס ומה נרוויח מ"מ הקושיא במקומו. והמעדני מלך נראה דביקש ליישבו דמ"מ כך דרך הגמרא לשנוי' תי' מרווח ברישא ואח"כ שנוי' דחיקא. ולכך ה"ל לשנויא בקושי' ראשונה בדתפס ואין זה מספיק ובפרט לדחות דברי הרי"ף דמי שקל בפלס השכל התי' אולי תי' זה דניזק אומר שמא יותר מרווח מהך תי' דתפס דתפיסה במשנה מאן דכר שמי'. ולכן היה נראה דהרא"ש ס"ל כדעת נ"י בהך מועד הזיק הגדול וזה אומר מועד הזיק הקטן ה"ל ממין טענה דשניהם מעלי' משלמין וה"ל כתבעו בק' הלואה ומודה לו בחמשין וא"כ ע"כ דסיפא איירי או דניזק טוען שמא או דמזיק טוען שמא דאל"כ איך קתני הממע"ה בהך בבא דמועד הזיק הגדול וזה אומר הקטן הא חייב ש"ד ישבע מבעיא ליה וגם מה קמ"ל דלא כסומכס דס"ל יחלוקו הא בהך לא פליג סומכס דמודה היכי דאיכא ש"ד כהנ"ל: ועכצ"ל או דניזק טוען שמא וה"ל טענת שמא וליכא שבועה או דמזיק טוען שמא ומשאיל"מ לא שייך הכא דלא ה"ל למידע וכמ"ש הש"ך לקמן בסי' ת' וק' א"כ ל"ל לר"פ כל צורך אריכות הפלפול מתיובתא דרבה ב"נ וכדומה ה"ל להקשות בקיצור ע"כ סיפא בברי ושמא וא"כ ע"כ מציעתא ורישא ג"כ בברי ושמא איירי או שהניזק או שהמזיק טוען שמא אבל בברי וברי לא מתוקמי. ועכצ"ל דעיקר דומי' דבעינן מרישא למציעתא אבל לא מסיפא וא"כ קושי' הרא"ש על נכון דלוקמי רישא ומציעתא בברי וברי ובתפס וסיפא בשמא וברי ואין נ"מ בדומיא דסיפא. (מיהו לפמ"ש התו' למ"ד חמשין ידענא חמשין לא ידענא פטור א"כ מ"מ אמאי ישבע הא יש לו מגו דטוען על מה שכופר לא ידענא ותי' דאין טוען ברצון לא ידענא דנראה כמשקר. לפ"ז כאן גבי נגיחות כיון בטוען שמא אם גדול או קטן הזיק לא דנין ביה משאיל"מ דלא ה"ל למדע א"כ אף בטוען ברי קטן הזיק פטור משבועה דיש לו מגו אינו יודע ולא שייך תי' התו' דבזו אינו נחשב כשקרן דלא ה"ל למידע. וא"כ ליכא כאן שבועה. ובזה י"ל ג"כ דברי הרי"ף דהרא"ש שפיר הקשה נוקי מציעתא בדתפס ולא סיפא דלכאורה מאי קשה הא אף דנימא סיפא ברי ושמא מ"מ בברי וברי ג"כ איירי דהא לא כי קתני א"כ במועד הזיק הגדול שבועה בעי ועכצ"ל דתפס וה"ל הילך כדעת הפוסקים דמשכון נמי איקרי הילך אך י"ל דליכא כאן שבועה כמ"ש דיש לו מגו אבל הרי"ף ס"ל מגו לאפטורי משבועה ל"א ועכצ"ל בדתפס ולק"מ ודוק) וכן צ"ל בתו' שם ד"ה לימא דהקשו דילמא ר"ג היא דמחייב שבועה: וק' א"כ אמאי הממע"ה ישבע מבעיא ליה וגם לא פליג סומכס וצ"ל דס"ל לתו' דה"ל הילך במה שמודה בתם כיון דשותף הוא בו ויכול להקדישו והוי כפקדון ודלא כש"ך לקמן בסי' ת' והא דמביא הש"ך ראיה מריש פ' הפרה דהקשו התו' בהא אפי' ניזק אומר ברי ומזיק שמא דנימא ביה משאיל"מ ותי' דלא ה"ל למידע או מודה בקנס פטור ולא תי' דה"ל הילך אין ראיה דודאי בתי' ראשון של תו' יש להבין דקארי לי' מאי קארי פשיטא דלא שייך בזו שבועה דהא אלו יודה יפטור. רק התו' ס"ל בתי' ראשון הואיל וסתמא קאמר אפי' ניזק אומר ברי משמע אפי' במועד וא"כ במועד שפיר ק' הא ה"ל משאיל"מ ולא שייך הילך כלל: ובהך תי' דמשני התו' דמיירי בתם ל"ל לתו' הילך כיון דבאמת אין כאן שבועה כלל דה"ל מודה בקנס ובפרט לחד אוקימתא בשבועות דס"ל לשמואל טען חיטין ושעורים והודה לו בא' פטור משבועה וא"כ הילך חייב כר"ת כמ"ש התו' בב"מ דף ה' ד"ה אי נמי ע"ש. והך קאמר שמואל אפי' ניזק אומר ברי כו' וא"כ ליכא לשנויא הילך דלשמואל הילך חייב והתו' ביקש לתרוצי מלתא דשמואל לכל אוקמתא ואין כאן ראיה משם אבל מכאן מוכח דס"ל לתי' דה"ל הילך. רק קשה תינח מציעתא סיפא מועד הזיק הגדול וזה אומר הקטן אפי' נימא דלא כנ"י מ"מ א"א לומר דר"ג היא דישבע מבעיא ליה וכאן ליכא הילך וע"כ צ"ל דס"ל לתו' כנ"י וא"כ בלא"ה צ"ל סיפא איירי בחד טוען שמא ומ"מ לא פריך ר"פ מיני' ש"מ דאין נ"מ בדומי' דסיפא ופריך התו' שפיר דנימא ר"ג היא ומציעתא הילך וא"כ הא מה מקום קושיא יש להרי"ף דס"ל דלא כנ"י כמ"ש לקמן סי' ת' דגם הרמב"ם לא ס"ל כוותיה ועיין מ"ש שם וא"כ ודאי דכל המשנה בעינן דומי' ואין כאן קושיא כלל דלא מרווחנא מידי אי נפרש מציעתא בדתפס וא"ש: ועוד היה מקום לתרץ דלכך לא מיקי ר"פ בקושיא דמציעתא איירי בדתפס משום דודאי לפרש הך משנה בתפס דוחק דתפס מאן דכר שמי' אך אם בלא"ה צריכין לומר אף דקתני במשנה הממע"ה מ"מ איירי דתפס הניזק א"כ אף בזו י"ל דתפס מתחילה קודם התביעה דכיון דבלא"ה איירי המשנה בכך דתפסו והיינו למ"ד פ"נ קנסא ק' קושית הרא"ש מה כל הסכסוך הא אף דיודה המזיק לכל דבריו יפטור. ושנויא של הרא"ש דיש עדים ולא ידעו מי נגח הוא דוחק כדפרכינן בפ' חזקת אי דאיכא עדים נחזי מה קאמרי ואף כאן הדוחק מבואר רק צ"ל כמ"ש המ"מ דמיירי בדתפס ובזו לא מהני מודה בקנס לגבי פ"נ קנסא ע"ש. וא"כ כיון דבלא"ה איירי דתפס שפיר י"ל דתיכף תפסו ולא הוי טענו בחיטין וכו' ולפ"ז ס"ל להרי"ף סתם גמרא דס"ל פ"נ קנסא משני בדתפס ובאמת קאי אף על המציעתא רק דלא פריך ממציעתא משום דיש לומר ראוי ליטול דבהא לא היה לו ברייתא להקשות מיניה וכמש"ל אבל באמת קאי על המציעתא אבל ר"פ דס"ל פ"נ ממון לא מצי לשנויא כלל בדתפס דתפיסה מאן דכר שמי' המוציא קתני ואי דבלא"ה באנו לכלל תפיסה מטעם מודה בקנס ר"פ לא ס"ל הך ולכך משני בניזק אומר שמא וכן סיפא בכך דלא ס"ל להרי"ף מ"ש רש"י ותו' תרתי ל"ל דודאי מצריך צריכי בכמה גווני כמ"ש התו' גופיה וסתמא דגמרא דמשני בדתפס ולא משני דניזק אומר שמא הוא לרבה ב"מ וכמ"ש דקי"ל אמר סומכס אפי' ברי וברי וא"כ כל המשנה בברי וברי איירי וא"ש:
segments.en: And if he seized it. This is the view of the Rif and Rambam. The Rosh, however, asks according to his approach that if so, the Gemara should also have established the middle clause as a case of seizure rather than as one where the injured party says he is uncertain and the tortfeasor says he is certain. The Shach writes to resolve this. Before considering his resolution, however, we must understand the Rosh's question itself. Why does the Rosh not ask the same question against his own approach? Let both clauses be established as cases where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor is certain. One must answer, as Rashi and Tosafot do, that if so the two clauses would be redundant. But if the Rif's explanation is that both clauses concern seizure, the same redundancy exists. It is true that the Rosh was careful on this point and wrote that the middle clause should have been established as a case of seizure and the final clause as a case of a definite claim against an uncertain one. Yet the need for this is unclear. What do we gain? The difficulty against Rabbah bar Mamal that the Mishnah does not deal with two definite claims remains. Surely the first, middle, and final clauses are all meant to parallel one another. As the Gemara itself explains, the final clause involves the injured party making a definite claim, the tortfeasor being uncertain, and seizure, while the middle clause has the reverse, the tortfeasor certain and the injured party uncertain, and the first clause again has the tortfeasor uncertain and the injured party certain. All the clauses thus contain some combination of definite and uncertain claims. If we reverse the explanations, the clauses are still parallel. The final clause would have the injured party uncertain and the tortfeasor certain, while the middle and first clauses would have the injured party certain and the tortfeasor uncertain, with the middle clause involving seizure. What, then, has been gained? The original difficulty remains. The Maadanei Melech apparently seeks to resolve this by saying that the way of the Gemara is to give the more comfortable explanation first and only afterward resort to a strained one. Thus, on the first difficulty the Gemara should have answered with seizure. This is not sufficient, especially as a basis for rejecting the Rif. Who can weigh the Gemara's answers so precisely as to say that the explanation involving uncertainty by the injured party is more comfortable than the explanation involving seizure? Seizure is itself entirely unmentioned in the Mishnah. It therefore appears that the Rosh follows the view of the Nimukei Yosef regarding the case where the claimant says that the larger mu'ad ox caused the damage and the other says that the smaller mu'ad ox caused it. Both obligations are paid from the owner's superior assets, and therefore the admission is of the same kind as the claim. It is comparable to one who claims one hundred as a loan and the defendant admits fifty. If so, the final clause necessarily concerns either an injured party who is uncertain or a tortfeasor who is uncertain. Otherwise, how could the Mishnah merely say that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant in the case where the claimant says the larger mu'ad caused the damage and the other says the smaller mu'ad caused it? The defendant would be liable for a Torah oath, and the Mishnah should have said that he must swear. Moreover, what would the Mishnah teach against Sumchus? Sumchus agrees that his division rule does not apply where a Torah oath exists, as explained above. We must therefore say either that the injured party is uncertain, in which case there is no definite claim upon which to impose an oath, or that the tortfeasor is uncertain. In the latter case the rule that one who cannot swear must pay does not apply because the tortfeasor had no reason to know which ox caused the damage, as the Shach writes below in siman 400. If so, why did Rav Pappa need all the lengthy analysis involving a supposed refutation of Rabbah bar Natan and the like? He could have asked much more simply: the final clause necessarily involves one party being uncertain. Therefore the middle and first clauses must also involve a definite and uncertain claim, whether the injured party or the tortfeasor is the uncertain one. They cannot be cases of two definite claims. We must consequently say that the required parallelism is primarily between the first and middle clauses, not between those clauses and the final clause. The Rosh's question is therefore sound. The Gemara could have established the first and middle clauses as cases of two definite claims together with seizure, while allowing the final clause to involve a definite and uncertain claim, since no full parallelism to the final clause is required. There is, however, another point. Tosafot write according to the view that one who says, "Fifty I know and fifty I do not know," is exempt, that even in a case of partial admission, why should he swear if he has a migo that he could have said concerning the denied portion, "I do not know"? They answer that a person does not willingly say, "I do not know," because that makes him appear dishonest. According to this, in a case of goring, where a person who says he does not know whether the larger or smaller ox caused the damage is not subject to the rule that one who cannot swear must pay because he had no reason to know, even one who says definitely that the smaller ox caused the damage should be exempt from an oath. He has a migo that he could say, "I do not know," and Tosafot's answer does not apply because such uncertainty would not make him appear dishonest in a matter he had no reason to know. If so, there may be no oath here at all. This also helps explain the Rif. The Rosh properly asks that the middle clause should have been established as a case of seizure rather than the final clause. At first glance, what is the question? Even if we say that the final clause involves a definite claim against uncertainty, the final clause also includes two definite claims because the Mishnah says, "No, rather," and in the case where the claimant says that the larger mu'ad caused the damage while the other says the smaller mu'ad caused it, an oath should be required. We would therefore still need seizure, since according to the authorities a pledge or property already in hand is heilech. Yet one may answer that there is no oath here because the defendant has a migo that he could have said he does not know, as just explained. But the Rif holds that a migo is not accepted to exempt one from an oath. If so, according to the Rif seizure is indeed required in the final clause, and the Rosh's question falls away. Examine this carefully. The same must be said concerning Tosafot there, s.v. leima. They ask why the Mishnah could not follow Rabban Gamliel, who obligates an oath where one claims wheat and the defendant admits barley. But then why does the Mishnah say only that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant? It should say that the defendant must swear. Also, Sumchus does not disagree where there is a Torah oath. We must therefore say that Tosafot regard the defendant's admission concerning the tam ox as heilech, because the injured party is already a partner in that ox and may consecrate his share. It is therefore comparable to a deposit already available to the claimant, contrary to the Shach's position below in siman 400. The Shach brings a proof from Tosafot at the beginning of chapter HaParah. Tosafot ask why, even where the injured party makes a definite claim and the tortfeasor is uncertain, we do not apply the rule that one who cannot swear must pay. They answer either that the tortfeasor had no reason to know or that an admission to a fine exempts him. Tosafot do not answer that the admission is heilech. This is no proof. Tosafot's first answer itself is difficult to understand. Why did the question arise at all? It is obvious that there can be no oath where, if the defendant admitted liability, he would be exempt as one who admits a fine. Rather, Tosafot's first answer must understand the Mishnah's general formulation to include even a mu'ad ox. In that case the rule that one who cannot swear must pay does apply, and there is no concept of heilech because payment from a mu'ad is taken from superior assets rather than from the body of the ox. In Tosafot's second answer, which establishes the case as one involving a tam, there is no need to invoke heilech because there is no oath at all, since an admission to the fine would exempt him. Moreover, according to one establishment in Shevuot, Shmuel holds that where one claims wheat and barley and the defendant admits one of them, he is exempt from an oath, while heilech itself creates liability according to Rabbenu Tam, as Tosafot write in Bava Metzia 5, s.v. i nami. Yet Shmuel himself is the one who says that the rule applies even where the injured party makes a definite claim, etc. Tosafot therefore needed an answer to Shmuel's statement that works according to every establishment. They could not rely on heilech, since according to Shmuel heilech may obligate rather than exempt. There is thus no proof from that passage. Here, however, the sugya does indicate that Tosafot's answer depends upon treating the tam ox as heilech. There remains a difficulty regarding the middle and final clauses. In the final clause, where the claimant says the larger mu'ad ox caused the damage and the defendant says the smaller mu'ad did, even if we disagree with the Nimukei Yosef, it is impossible to say that the Mishnah follows Rabban Gamliel unless we say that an oath is required, because there is no heilech with respect to a mu'ad. We must therefore say that Tosafot agree with the Nimukei Yosef that this is an admission of the same kind as the claim. If so, the final clause independently must involve one party being uncertain. Yet Rav Pappa does not derive his argument from that clause. This shows that parallelism to the final clause is not essential. Tosafot's question is therefore sound: perhaps the Mishnah follows Rabban Gamliel, while the middle clause involves heilech. In that case, however, what room is there for the Rosh's question against the Rif, who does not accept the Nimukei Yosef's view, as I will explain below in siman 400, and Rambam likewise does not accept it? According to the Rif, full parallelism throughout the Mishnah can indeed be required, and the objection disappears. There is another possible resolution. Rav Pappa does not establish the middle clause as involving seizure because it is certainly strained to interpret a Mishnah that says only that the claimant must bring proof as secretly referring to property already seized by the claimant. Seizure is not mentioned at all. But if, independently, we must say that even though the Mishnah says that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant it nevertheless concerns a case where the injured party had seized the ox, then it is reasonable to say that the seizure occurred from the outset before the claims were made. Once we already know that the Mishnah deals with seizure, we can use that fact throughout. This is relevant according to the view that half damages are a fine. The Rosh asks how the Mishnah can involve the owner's admission, since even if he admitted every detail he would be exempt as one who admits a fine. The Rosh's answer, that there were witnesses but they did not know which ox gored, is strained, like the Gemara's question in Bava Batra: if there are witnesses, let us see what they say. Here too, the difficulty is obvious. The Maggid Mishneh therefore explains that the injured party had seized the ox. Seizure prevents the tortfeasor's admission from exempting him from half damages even according to the view that half damages are a fine. Once the Mishnah must in any event be understood as involving seizure, it is reasonable to say that the injured party seized before making his claim, and then the rule of claiming wheat and admitting barley does not apply. Accordingly, the Rif may hold that the anonymous Gemara, which follows the ruling that half damages are a fine, answers with seizure, and that answer in truth applies to the middle clause as well. The Gemara does not ask from the middle clause because it could have answered that the injured party is fit to take there and has nothing, since no baraita was cited to contradict such an explanation, as I wrote above. But in substance the seizure answer can apply there too. Rav Pappa, by contrast, holds that half damages are compensatory and therefore has no independent reason to introduce seizure into the Mishnah. For him, seizure remains unmentioned and strained, so he cannot use that answer. He therefore establishes the middle clause as one where the injured party is uncertain. The same applies to the final clause. The Rif need not accept Rashi and Tosafot's claim that the clauses would then be redundant, because many distinctions make each clause necessary, as Tosafot themselves discuss. The anonymous Gemara that answers with seizure follows Rabbah bar Mamal and, as explained, can maintain that Sumchus applies even to two definite claims. The entire Mishnah can therefore remain a case of two definite claims. Everything is properly explained.

segments.he: ויש להרי"ף ראיה ברורה דתפס קאי גם על הרישא דצ"ל הא דמוקי ר"פ מציעתא בניזק אומר שמא ומזיק אומר ברי והרישא להיפוך ניזק אומר ברי ומזיק שמא ואף דקתני לא כי בברי וברי נמי איירי רק בהא לא פליג סומכס וכל רבותא דקמ"ל הוא בטוען שמא וכמ"ש התו' והמהרש"א ולכאורה קשה מה דוחקיה דר"פ לומר רישא ומציעתא הם בדמיון בלתי שוה בזה המזיק שמא ובזה הניזק שמא וגם קשה לומר דבמ"מ אמר סומכס אפי' ניזק שמא ומזיק ברי כמ"ש התו' ולא מוקי רישא ומציעתא בשמא ושמא בהא יחלקו סומכס ורבנן: ובאמת בניזק אומר שמא ומזיק אומר ברי נמי איירי וא"ש לא כי אך בזה באמת לית רבותא דלא יחלוק סומכס ודוחק לומר דא"כ כל הרישא מיותר דמאי קמ"ל אי להורות דאמר סומכס בשמא ושמא טובא משניות איכא דס"ל לסומכוס כן בריש הפרה ומשנה דשאלה ושכורה והמחליף דיחלוקו בשמא ושמא. ואי להודיע דאף בהא פליגי רבנן השתא במציעתא דאיכא מ"מ ס"ל לחכמים הממע"ה כ"ש ברישא דאיכא כופר הכל: ולכך צ"ל דרישא בניזק אומר ברי ומזיק שמא וקמ"ל דאפי' בהו ס"ל לחכמים הממע"ה דלא כסומכס וא"כ אף מציעתא ע"כ בהא מתפרש דזהו דוחק כמ"ש מהרש"א דלולי דדייקי לא כי הוי מוקמינן הכל בשמא ושמא וזה מבואר דלא כמ"ש: וצ"ל דבשלמא ברישא אף דעיקר פלוגתא דסומכס וחכמים איירי בברי ושמא מ"מ קתני לא כי דאפי' בברי וברי מיירי דקמ"ל אפי' בשור מועד דהיה רודף מ"מ ס"ל לחכמים דתלינן בסלע כמ"ש הרמב"ם ולאפוקי מדעת היש"ש וסתמא קתני שור אפי' מועד. אבל במציעתא אי איירי בשמא ושמא פלוגת' למה קתני לא כי להור' דבניזק שמא ומזיק ברי נמי איירי מה נ"מ בדינא פשיטא דהא לא חולק סומכס כלל ואין כאן נ"מ כלל במה דקתני לא כי אלא וודאי דאיירי בניזק שמא ומזיק ברי דבהא ס"ל לסומכס יחלוקו ולחכמים הממע"ה. ולפ"ז דע"כ איירי סיפא בניזק אומר שמא ומזיק ברי דהא קתני לא כי דאפי' לרבה ב"מ דס"ל רישא מיירי בברי וברי צ"ל דס"ל מציעתא איירי עכ"פ דמזיק אומר ברי דהוי דומיה בחד צד: אבל ודאי דמציעתא איירי בשמא ושמא א"א כמ"ש דהא קתני לא כי א"כ קשה לאביי דס"ל כמ"ש התו' בפ' י"נ דף קל"ה ד"ה אביי דס"ל לאביי אפי' במקום דלא ה"ל למידע כלל וכלל מ"מ ברי ושמא ברי עדיף א"כ הך דרישא דמיירי דניזק אומר ברי ומזיק שמא ס"ל לחכמים הממע"ה הא ברי עדיף ומכ"ש דקשה במציעתא דע"כ איירי. בניזק אומר שמא ומזיק ברי וס"ל לסומכס יחלוקו וק' קושית התו' הא ברי עדיף ותי' התו' דלא ה"ל למדע לא שייך לאביי והיא קושיא עצומה. ולכך ס"ל להרי"ף כמ"ש דהשתא דאמרי' דתפס אף מציעתא א"ש אפי' בברי וברי וא"כ לא קשיא מידי לאביי דהוא מפרש מציעתא בברי וברי ובהא פליג סומכס ולא קשיא מרבה ב"נ דתפס וא"ש. וזהו לענ"ד ראיה ברורה ועצומה לדברי הרי"ף והתו' בפ' המניח דס"ל דלא קאי תפס ארישא אזלו לשיטתן דס"ל בפ' הפרה דאף אביי ס"ל במקום דלא ה"ל למידע לא אמרי' ברי עדיף וא"כ לק"מ אבל הרי"ף ס"ל כמ"ש התו' ב"ב כמש"ל ויש לו ראיה ברורה:
segments.en: And there is a clear proof for the Rif that the seizure explanation applies to the first clause as well. We must explain Rav Pappa's establishment of the middle clause as one where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor is certain, and the first clause in the reverse, with the injured party certain and the tortfeasor uncertain. Although the Mishnah says "No, rather," which ordinarily indicates two definite claims, Tosafot and Maharsha explain that the clause includes such a case but that Sumchus's disagreement is relevant only to the case of uncertainty. At first glance, why was Rav Pappa forced to make the first and middle clauses only imperfectly parallel, with uncertainty on opposite sides? It would seem simpler to establish both as cases where both parties are uncertain. In such a case Sumchus and the Sages disagree directly. It is true that the middle clause also includes the case where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor is certain, which explains the words "No, rather," but there would then be no novelty in saying that Sumchus does not require division in that subcase. One could hardly say that the entire first clause is superfluous, because if it comes merely to teach that Sumchus requires division where both are uncertain, many Mishnayot already establish that rule, such as the beginning of chapter HaParah and the Mishnayot concerning the borrowed and rented animals and concerning an exchange. Nor is it necessary to teach that the Sages disagree even there. If, in the middle clause where there is partial admission, the Sages nevertheless say that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant, then all the more so in the first clause where the defendant totally denies liability. We must therefore say that the first clause concerns an injured party making a definite claim and a tortfeasor who is uncertain. It teaches that even there the Sages apply the rule that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant, contrary to Sumchus. The middle clause must correspondingly be understood in that way as well to the extent the wording allows, which is strained, as Maharsha notes. Were it not for the implication of "No, rather," we would have established the whole matter as uncertainty on both sides. There is, however, a way to explain the wording. In the first clause, although the main dispute between Sumchus and the Sages concerns the case where the injured party is certain and the tortfeasor uncertain, the Mishnah still says "No, rather" because it also includes two definite claims. It teaches that even where the ox was a mu'ad that was pursuing the injured animal, the Sages nevertheless allow the tortfeasor to say that the animal was struck by a rock, as Rambam rules, contrary to the view of Maharshal. The Mishnah says simply "an ox," which includes a mu'ad. But in the middle clause, if the actual dispute were only where both parties were uncertain, why would the Mishnah say "No, rather" merely to include an additional case where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor certain? There would be no practical dispute in that additional case, since Sumchus too would agree that the possessor's definite claim prevails. The phrase would teach nothing. Therefore the middle clause itself must involve a case where the injured party is uncertain and the tortfeasor certain, and even there Sumchus requires division while the Sages apply the rule that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant.
